lessons.title: Synchronous dependencies: availability and tail latency
lessons.summary: Predict how waiting on several required services erodes availability, tail latency and capacity.
lessons.body:
When one service needs another to do something, it has two basic choices. It can **ask and wait** (synchronous), or it can **leave a note and move on** (asynchronous). Almost every messaging system you will meet in this module exists to make the second option reliable.

## Synchronous: request and wait

In a synchronous call, the caller sends a request (usually HTTP or gRPC) and logically waits for a response or timeout; a nonblocking client need not block an operating-system thread.

```
Checkout ──HTTP──▶ Payments ──▶ Fraud
   ▲                  │            │
   └──── waits ───────┴── waits ───┘
```

This is simple and gives you an immediate answer, which is exactly what you want when the user is waiting for that answer: "was my card accepted?"

But synchronous chains have three structural weaknesses:

- **Availability multiplies.** If Checkout requires three services that are each 99.9% available and their failures are independent, all three must be up at once, so together they are only about 99.7% available. Correlated failures change this calculation, and Checkout has its own failure modes. That is about 26 hours of downtime a year instead of 8.8.
- **Latency adds up.** Sequential dependent calls add their durations; parallel fan-out waits for the required critical path, and tail latency (p99) gets worse as you add hops, because the slowest dependency dominates. If a request touches 5 services with independent delays and each is slow 1% of the time, the request hits at least one slow call about 4.9% of the time: tail slowness becomes more frequent at the request level; exact quantiles depend on the full latency distributions.
- **Load is coupled.** A spike at the front door hits every downstream service at the same instant. If Fraud can only handle 500 requests a second, Checkout can only handle 500 requests a second.

Both numbers come from one rule of probability: when events are independent, the chance that all of them happen is the product of their separate chances. A request that needs every dependency succeeds only when all of them are up, and is fast only when every call is fast.

```formula reference
A_chain = A_1 × A_2 × A_3
P_slow = 1 − (1 − p)^k
where
A_chain: the availability of the chain: the fraction of time all three required dependencies are up together, ignoring Checkout's own failures
A_1: the availability of the first dependency (Payments), as a fraction; 99.9% is 0.999
A_2: the availability of the second dependency (Inventory), as a fraction
A_3: the availability of the third dependency (Fraud), as a fraction
P_slow: the probability that a request hits at least one slow call
p: the probability that any one call is slow, as a fraction; 1% is 0.01
k: the number of independent calls the request must wait for
^: to the power of; (1 − p)^k is the chance that all k calls are fast
In words: multiply the availabilities of required dependencies, so three 99.9% services give about 99.7%; and a request that waits for five calls, each slow 1% of the time, is slow about 5% of the time.
```

Both relationships assume independence. Shared causes (one database, one network link, one bad deploy) make failures and slow calls happen together, so real systems can be better or worse than these numbers, and you should measure. The practical lesson does not depend on the exact figure: every extra *required* hop on the synchronous path adds its own downtime and its own chance of a slow response.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a journey with connecting trains
> A trip that needs three connecting trains only works if all three run. Each line might be reliable on its own, but the more connections you need, the more often something spoils the whole trip. If you wait on a platform for several friends arriving on different trains, you leave when the *last* one arrives.
>
> **How it maps:** Each train is a required dependency. Needing every connection is a series dependency, so the journey fails more often than any one line (availability multiplies). Waiting for every friend is parallel fan-out: the slowest arrival sets your departure time (tail latency).
>
> **Where it stops:** Trains on one network often fail together (one signal fault, one strike), which is exactly the shared-cause case that breaks the independence assumption. And a train timetable is fixed, whereas a service can time out, retry or degrade gracefully rather than simply waiting.

## Key takeaways

- A synchronous request waits logically for a result; it need not block an operating-system thread.
- Independent required dependencies multiply availability, while parallel fan-out exposes the slowest required call.
- Shared failures break the independence assumption, so measure the actual critical path.

## Further reading

- [Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling)
- [Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/)

questions.prompt: Checkout requires successful responses from Payments, Inventory and Fraud. Each service can fail independently. A colleague says adding Fraud cannot reduce availability because Payments was already the least available dependency. Which explanation is right?

options.text: Correct: only the least available dependency affects checkout
options.explanation: Wrong. A failure of any required service can fail checkout, including a failure while every other service is healthy.

options.text: Adding Fraud creates redundancy
options.explanation: Wrong. Redundancy needs alternatives that can serve the same purpose. Fraud is another required result.

options.text: Fraud adds another way for checkout to fail
options.explanation: Correct. Checkout needs every dependency to succeed. An independent Fraud outage can fail requests that would otherwise have succeeded.

options.text: The answer is always found by adding outage percentages
options.explanation: Wrong. Overlapping outages must not be counted twice. Independence permits a product model; shared causes require a different analysis.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify the success condition: all three required responses must succeed.
2. Consider a Fraud outage while Payments and Inventory are healthy. Checkout now fails, so Fraud adds exposure.
3. The exact combined availability depends on each service and how failures overlap. Independence gives a useful model, but shared networks or databases can correlate failures.
4. Move work off the response path only when the product does not need its result before responding.

questions.prompt: A product page calls 10 backend services **in parallel** and waits for all of them before rendering. Each service answers in about 50 ms 99% of the time, but 1% of its calls take about 1 second, independently of the others. Users report that roughly 1 page load in 10 takes about a second. Every service dashboard shows only 1% slow calls. What explains the gap?

options.text: Measurement noise: if each service is slow 1% of the time, pages must be slow about 1% of the time
options.explanation: Wrong. That would hold if the page waited for one particular service. It waits for all ten, so it is slow whenever **any** one of them is slow, which is far more likely than one specific call being slow.

options.text: The services must be slow together, because a page is only slow when all 10 calls are slow
options.explanation: Wrong. All ten being slow at once would be vanishingly rare (0.01 multiplied by itself ten times). The page needs only one slow call to be slow, because it waits for every result.

options.text: The page waits for the slowest of 10 calls, so it is slow if any one is slow: about 1 load in 10
options.explanation: Correct. All ten calls are fast only about 90% of the time (0.99 multiplied by itself ten times is about 0.904), so roughly 9.6% of page loads include at least one 1-second call. This is tail amplification: per-service tails become common at the page level.

options.text: Parallel calls add their latencies, so ten 50 ms calls take 500 ms and push the page towards a second
options.explanation: Wrong. Parallel calls overlap; the page waits for the slowest one, not the sum. Adding durations applies to sequential, dependent calls.

questions.workedExample:
1. The page waits for all ten results in parallel, so one slow required result delays the page.
2. Each dashboard measures one service. The page is exposed to the slow-call risk of every required service, so its slow requests can be much more common.
3. Parallel durations overlap; sequential dependent durations add. These are different critical paths.
4. Consider omitting optional results after a timeout or moving unnecessary response-path work to a queue. Hedged requests can reduce some tail delays but add load and require safe duplicate handling; they need workload-specific controls.

lessons.title: What asynchronous messaging decouples
lessons.summary: Separate temporal, rate, location and fan-out decoupling without losing sight of the message contract.
lessons.body:
Asynchronous messaging separates accepting work from finishing it. A queue carries a command to its intended handler; a topic can announce a fact to several independent subscribers.

For example, publishing one `OrderPlaced` event lets email, loyalty and warehouse services subscribe independently. Sending a separate command to every team instead makes the producer maintain that list of handlers. Pub/sub is explored later in the module.

## Asynchronous: send and carry on

In asynchronous communication, the producer hands a **message** to an intermediary (a broker) and can continue after the required broker acknowledgement without waiting for processing. A consumer picks the message up later, maybe milliseconds later, maybe hours.

```
Checkout ─▶ [ queue ] ─▶ Email worker
   │
   └─▶ responds to user at once
```

With durable queues, suitable publish acknowledgement and retention settings, the broker retains the message, so the producer and consumer do not need to be running at the same time. This is the key idea: **the queue decouples the two sides in time**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen
> A waiter clips an order ticket to the rail and goes back to the tables. Whichever cook is free takes the next ticket. During the lunch rush tickets pile up, and the cooks work through them at their own pace.
>
> **How it maps:** The waiter is the producer, the rail is the broker and the cooks are consumers. The waiter does not wait for the food (asynchronous), does not need a particular cook to be standing there (temporal decoupling), can clip tickets faster than they are cooked (rate decoupling) and never needs to know which cook will take one (location decoupling).
>
> **Where it stops:** A paper ticket can fall off the rail; a broker only keeps a message safe if it is configured to persist and acknowledge it. One ticket goes to one cook, so telling the bar *and* the kitchen needs a copy for each, which is what a topic adds. And the ticket is still a contract: a cook cannot read a ticket written in a new shorthand.

> [!note] Message vs event vs command
> A **command message** asks for something to happen ("SendReceiptEmail"). An **event message** states that something happened ("OrderPlaced"). Both travel as messages. Commands usually have one intended handler; events can have many. You will see why this matters in the pub/sub and event-driven lessons.

## The kinds of decoupling

"Decoupling" gets used loosely. It helps to separate it into distinct properties:

| Kind | What it means |
|---|---|
| Temporal | Consumer can be down when producer sends |
| Rate | Each side runs at its own speed |
| Location | Producer doesn't know consumer's address |
| Fan-out | Add consumers without changing producer |

A direct HTTP request does not by itself buffer work during consumer outages or fan it out; service discovery, proxies and other infrastructure can hide physical consumer addresses. A queue gives you the first three. A publish/subscribe topic adds the fourth.

What a queue does **not** decouple is the **message format**. If the producer changes the shape of the payload, consumers still break. Contracts and schema evolution (for example, Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry) remain your problem.

## Brokers you will meet

- **Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus**: message queues. A message is handed to one consumer and deleted once acknowledged.
- **Amazon SNS, Google Pub/Sub**: publish/subscribe. One message is copied to many subscribers.
- **Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Redpanda**: distributed logs. Messages are appended and retained; consumers track their own position and can replay.

The next lessons take each family in turn.

## Key takeaways

- Durability, publish acknowledgement and retention let a consumer process work after the producer has moved on.
- Queues decouple time, rate and consumer addresses; pub/sub also lets new subscribers join without changing the producer.
- The payload remains a contract: asynchronous transport does not make incompatible schemas safe.

## Further reading

- [What is a message queue? (AWS)](https://aws.amazon.com/message-queue/)
- [Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/)

questions.prompt: Which of these is the **main** thing a durable message queue gives you that a direct HTTP call does not?

options.text: Temporal decoupling: the consumer can be offline when the producer sends
options.explanation: Correct. The broker stores the message durably until a consumer is ready, so producer and consumer no longer need to be up at the same moment.

options.text: Freedom to change the message format without breaking consumers
options.explanation: Wrong. A queue does not decouple schemas. If the producer changes the payload shape, consumers still break. You need versioned schemas or a schema registry for that.

options.text: Lower end-to-end latency for each piece of work
options.explanation: Wrong. A broker adds at least one extra hop and often a polling delay, so the work usually completes later, not sooner. What gets faster is the producer's response, not the work itself.

options.text: Strong consistency between producer and consumer state
options.explanation: Wrong. Asynchronous messaging makes the consumer's state lag behind the producer's. It gives you eventual consistency, not strong consistency.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through what a queue physically does:

1. The producer writes a message to the broker, and the broker persists it.
2. The producer gets an acknowledgement from the **broker**, not from the consumer, and moves on.
3. The consumer reads the message whenever it is next running.

Step 2 is the key: the producer depends only on the broker being up. If the consumer is mid-deploy or has crashed, messages simply wait. That is temporal decoupling. Latency, schema compatibility and consistency are unchanged or made worse.

questions.prompt: After checkout, the orders service sends three messages: `SendReceiptEmail` to the email queue, `AwardPoints` to the loyalty queue and `ReserveStock` to the warehouse queue. Every new team that wants to react to orders needs a change and a redeploy of the orders service. Which redesign best addresses this?

options.text: Bundle the three commands into one message so there is only one send to maintain
options.explanation: Wrong. The orders service would still know every consumer and what each must do. Adding a fourth team still means changing the bundle and redeploying orders.

options.text: Publish a single `OrderPlaced` event to a topic and let each team subscribe and decide what to do with it
options.explanation: Correct. An event states a fact rather than instructing a particular handler. The publisher no longer knows who reacts, so new teams add a subscription without touching the orders service: fan-out decoupling.

options.text: Let each downstream team poll the orders database for new rows
options.explanation: Wrong. This removes the sends but couples every team to the orders table's internal schema and adds polling load to the orders database. The schema becomes an accidental public contract.

options.text: Replace the queues with synchronous HTTP calls so failures are visible to orders
options.explanation: Wrong. That re-couples availability, latency and load: a slow warehouse would now slow checkout. It also keeps the orders service aware of every consumer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Spot the smell: the producer is sending **commands**, each addressed to one specific handler. So the producer must know every consumer.
2. Ask what the producer actually knows: *an order was placed*. That is an **event**.
3. Publish `OrderPlaced` once to a pub/sub topic.
4. Email, loyalty and warehouse each subscribe and translate the event into their own work.
5. A new fraud team? It adds a subscription. The orders service is unchanged.

Commands still have their place (one intended handler, for example `ShipOrder` to the warehouse), but facts that many teams care about should be events.

questions.prompt: A team replaces a direct HTTP call from Orders to Invoicing with a single SQS queue that Invoicing consumes. Which kinds of decoupling have they gained? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fan-out: a new Analytics service can also receive every order without changing Orders
options.explanation: Wrong. A queue gives each message to **one** consumer. If Analytics read from the same queue it would compete with Invoicing and steal some of its messages. Fan-out needs a topic, such as SNS feeding a queue per subscriber.

options.text: Temporal: Invoicing can be down while Orders keeps sending
options.explanation: Correct. SQS stores the messages durably, so Orders only needs the queue to be available. Invoicing catches up when it returns.

options.text: Format: Invoicing keeps working if Orders renames payload fields
options.explanation: Wrong. A queue carries bytes; it does nothing about schemas. Renamed fields still break Invoicing. That needs versioned schemas and compatibility rules.

options.text: Rate: Orders can burst above Invoicing's processing speed
options.explanation: Correct. The backlog builds in the queue and Invoicing drains it at its own pace. This is queue-based load levelling.

options.text: Location: Orders needs only the queue's URL, not Invoicing's hosts
options.explanation: Correct. Invoicing can move, scale or change its address and Orders never notices, because both sides only know the queue.

questions.workedExample:
Go through the four kinds of decoupling from the lesson, plus schema:

| Kind | Queue gives it? |
|---|---|
| Temporal | Yes |
| Rate | Yes |
| Location | Yes |
| Fan-out | No, needs a topic |
| Format | No, never |

1. Temporal, rate and location all come from the broker sitting in the middle and storing messages.
2. Fan-out needs one **copy** per consumer. A point-to-point queue makes no copies.
3. A plain queue does not supply schema compatibility; schema tooling and compatibility rules must be explicitly designed.

lessons.title: Absorb a burst: backlog and drain time
lessons.summary: Predict how a burst builds a backlog, why only spare capacity drains it and how long the last message waits.
lessons.body:
A durable queue can hold a temporary traffic spike while a smaller worker fleet catches up. The useful question is how long users must wait, and whether the fleet can ever catch up.

## Load levelling

The most common practical reason to add a queue is to protect a slow or fragile component from bursts. This is the **queue-based load levelling** pattern.

Imagine an image-thumbnail service. Uploads arrive in bursts: 2,000 per second for 30 seconds after a marketing email, then 50 per second for the rest of the hour. Each worker can process 100 images per second.

```
 arrivals/s
 2000 ┤ ████
      │ ████
      │ ████
  200 ┤ ████ - - - - - - - - - workers
   50 ┤ ████▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁
      └──────────────────────▶ time
```

Without a queue, you need 20 workers (2,000 ÷ 100) sitting mostly idle to survive the peak. With a queue and 2 workers (200 per second capacity), the backlog grows while arrivals exceed capacity, and shrinks only by the capacity left over once new arrivals are served:

This fixed-rate estimate assumes an initially empty queue, a burst faster than processing, and post-burst arrivals slower than processing. It ignores startup delays and variation between jobs.

```formula reference
B = (λ_burst − μ) × T_burst
T_drain = B / (μ − λ_after)
where
B: the backlog: messages waiting in the queue when the burst ends
λ_burst: lambda, the arrival rate during the burst, in messages per second
μ: mu, the processing capacity of all workers together, in messages per second
T_burst: how long the burst lasts, in seconds
T_drain: the time after the burst until the queue is empty again, in seconds
λ_after: lambda, the arrival rate after the burst, in messages per second
In words: during a burst the queue grows by the excess of arrivals over capacity for as long as the burst lasts; afterwards it drains only at the spare capacity, so new arrivals slow the recovery.
```

In the thumbnail example the queue gains 1,800 messages a second for 30 seconds, leaving about 54,000 waiting. Afterwards the workers still have to serve 50 new uploads a second, so only 150 a second of their 200 is spare: the queue takes about 6 minutes to empty, not the 4.5 minutes you get by dividing the backlog by full capacity.

Those 4.5 minutes do mean something: in first-in, first-out (FIFO) order, the last message of the burst waits roughly as long as the workers take to clear the 54,000 ahead of it, about 270 seconds. The queue is empty only later, because new arrivals keep joining behind it.

So you trade **latency** (the longest wait is about 4.5 minutes, and the queue returns to empty after about 6) for **cost and stability** (10× fewer workers in this idealised fixed-rate model; consumer admission and downstream capacity still need protection). That trade is acceptable when the product permits the resulting delay, including an explicit pending-job experience.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a bath with the tap on and the plug half out
> Turn the tap on full and the water level rises even though the plughole is draining. Turn the tap down to a trickle and the bath empties, but only as fast as the plughole beats the trickle. Leave the tap running faster than the plughole on average and the bath eventually overflows.
>
> **How it maps:** The tap is the arrival rate, the plughole is the workers' total capacity and the water level is the backlog. The level rises at the difference between them during the burst and falls only at the spare capacity afterwards, which is why recovery is slower than "backlog ÷ capacity".
>
> **Where it stops:** Water has no order, so the bath says nothing about how long the *last* message waits in FIFO order. Real worker capacity also varies with message size and downstream health. And a bath overflows visibly, whereas a queue can grow silently until retention deletes old messages, which is why you alarm on depth and oldest-message age.

> [!warning] A queue is not infinite capacity
> Load levelling only works if the **average** arrival rate is below the processing rate. If arrivals average 250 per second and you can do 200, the backlog grows forever. A queue hides overload; it does not fix it. Always alarm on queue depth and on the age of the oldest message.

## Key takeaways

- During overload, the backlog grows by the difference between arrivals and processing capacity.
- After a burst, new arrivals consume capacity too; only spare capacity drains the backlog.
- Average arrivals must remain below processing capacity: a queue cannot cure sustained overload.

## Further reading

- [Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling)
- [Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library)](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/)

questions.prompt: A burst leaves a FIFO queue full of jobs. Workers keep processing at a steady rate, while new jobs arrive more slowly and join the back. A teammate predicts the queue becomes empty as soon as the last job from the original burst finishes. What is wrong with that prediction?

options.text: Nothing: finishing the burst always empties the queue
options.explanation: Wrong. New jobs have joined behind the burst while it was being processed.

options.text: The burst can finish while later arrivals still remain
options.explanation: Correct. FIFO places new jobs behind the original burst. Emptying the entire queue takes longer because those jobs also need processing.

options.text: A queue can never recover once a burst exceeds capacity
options.explanation: Wrong. A temporary burst can be drained when later arrival rates stay below processing capacity.

options.text: New arrivals always delay the last original job under FIFO
options.explanation: Wrong. Under the stated FIFO and fixed-rate assumptions they join behind it; they delay the return to an empty queue.

questions.workedExample:
1. Mark the jobs already present at the end of the burst.
2. Under FIFO, workers process those jobs before the new jobs joining behind them.
3. When the last marked job finishes, later arrivals can still be waiting.
4. Only spare processing capacity reduces the total backlog. As continuing arrivals approach processing capacity, emptying the queue takes longer; sustained arrivals above capacity prevent recovery.

questions.prompt: A PDF-rendering queue grows during each working day and shrinks overnight, but every morning starts with more unfinished work than the previous morning. Assume no failed jobs, changing job sizes or retention expiry. What is the right diagnosis and response?

options.text: The workers cannot clear a full day's arrivals; increase effective capacity or reduce admitted work
options.explanation: Correct. Quiet hours are not making up the daytime deficit. Capacity needs headroom to clear the recurring workload and recover from incidents.

options.text: Load levelling is working because the queue shrinks overnight
options.explanation: Wrong. Shrinking for part of the cycle is insufficient when each complete cycle leaves a larger backlog.

options.text: Raise the queue's maximum size to solve the problem
options.explanation: Wrong. More storage delays overflow but does not change the accumulating capacity deficit.

options.text: FIFO ordering guarantees the backlog will eventually disappear
options.explanation: Wrong. Ordering determines which jobs run first, not whether enough jobs can be completed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare the same point in successive workload cycles, rather than only the daytime peak.
2. A rising morning baseline means each day leaves unfinished work behind.
3. Increase effective processing capacity, reduce admissions or reduce work per job. Check downstream limits before adding workers.
4. Monitor oldest-message age and retention as well as depth; a queue cannot preserve unfinished work indefinitely.

lessons.title: Convert average queue depth into waiting time
lessons.summary: Use Little's Law with a stable queue and a consistent system boundary.
lessons.body:
Queue depth is a count, but users experience a delay. Little's Law connects the two. Decide what you count before using it: messages still waiting correspond to queue wait, while waiting plus in-flight messages correspond to total time in that system.

## Little's Law: a useful sanity check

Little's Law says that, in a stable system (one where, over time, items leave as fast as they arrive), the average number of items in it equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends in it. Rearranged, it tells you the average wait from two numbers a dashboard already shows:

```formula essential
L = λ × W
W = L / λ
where
L: the average number of items in the system; for a queue, the average queue depth, in messages
λ: lambda, the average arrival rate, in messages per second
W: the average time an item spends in the system, in seconds (s)
s: seconds
In words: average depth equals arrival rate times average wait, so depth divided by arrival rate gives the average wait.
```

So a queue that receives 400 messages per second and holds a steady 12,000 makes each message wait about 30 seconds on average. This turns "queue depth" (which dashboards show) into "delay" (which users feel).

The same depth can mean very different delays. 12,000 messages waiting in a queue that receives 4,000 a second is only about a 3-second wait; in one that receives 40 a second it is about 5 minutes. Depth alone does not tell you whether users are waiting: you need the rate as well.

Little's Law holds for long-run averages in a stable system, whatever the number of consumers or the order they serve messages in. While a queue is growing during a burst, the momentary numbers need not match it.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: people inside a café
> If about two customers walk into a café each minute and there are usually about ten people inside, each customer must be staying about five minutes on average. You can work that out from the door counter and a head count, without timing anyone.
>
> **How it maps:** The head count is the queue depth (L), customers per minute is the arrival rate (λ) and the average stay is the wait (W). Choosing whether to count only people waiting for coffee, or also people sitting down, is choosing the system boundary.
>
> **Where it stops:** The estimate only works when the café is in a steady state; at opening time, when it is filling up, a head count and the door rate do not give the stay. And it gives the *average* stay, not how long the unluckiest customer waited.

## Key takeaways

- In a stable system, average depth divided by average arrival rate gives average time spent inside the measured boundary.
- Waiting-only depth measures time before processing; including active work measures the whole residence time.
- Use long-run averages; a snapshot taken during burst growth need not obey the steady-state estimate.

## Further reading

- [Little's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little%27s_law)
- [Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library)](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/)

questions.prompt: Two stable queues have the same long-run average number of messages waiting, excluding messages already being processed. Queue B receives and completes messages much faster than queue A. What does Little's Law imply?

options.text: Their average waiting times must be equal
options.explanation: Wrong. Depth counts messages; it does not measure how quickly that population turns over.

options.text: Queue A has a longer average waiting time
options.explanation: Correct. At the same average depth, slower throughput means messages spend longer waiting.

options.text: Queue B must have the longer wait because it is busier
options.explanation: Wrong. Both queues are stable and have equal average depth; faster turnover means less average waiting.

options.text: Nothing can be inferred without counting workers
options.explanation: Wrong. For a stable system, matched average depth and throughput determine average time within the chosen boundary.

questions.workedExample:
1. Match the measurement boundary: both depths count waiting messages only.
2. Little's Law relates average population, throughput and average time inside that boundary.
3. The same population turning over faster means a shorter average wait. It does not predict each message's wait or the worst case.
4. Use long-run stable averages, not a burst snapshot. Oldest-message age is a separate useful signal; SQS can exclude some repeatedly received poison messages from that metric.

lessons.title: Choose async work and keep the user informed
lessons.summary: Place work according to the response users need, then handle pending results, failures and tracing.
lessons.body:
An asynchronous design changes the promise the product makes. Accepting a job means it will be attempted later; it does not mean its database write or external side effect has already succeeded.

## When to choose which

| Situation | Better fit |
|---|---|
| User needs the answer now | Sync |
| Work can finish later | Async |
| Downstream is slow or flaky | Async |
| Strong read-after-write needed | Sync |
| Many systems react to one fact | Async (pub/sub) |

A common shape is **sync at the edge, async inside**. The checkout API synchronously authorises the payment (the user needs to know), writes the order, then reliably publishes `OrderPlaced`, for example via an outbox committed with the order. Email, analytics, loyalty points and warehouse picking all happen asynchronously.

## The costs of going async

Asynchrony is not free. It moves complexity rather than removing it:

- **Eventual consistency.** The user may see "order placed" before the loyalty points appear. The UI and product need to tolerate that.
- **No direct error path.** If the email worker fails, it cannot return an HTTP 500 error to the user. You need retries, dead-letter queues and alerts instead.
- **Duplicate and out-of-order delivery.** Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent. Later lessons cover this in depth.
- **Harder debugging.** A request's story is split across processes and time. You need correlation IDs and distributed tracing (for example, propagating a W3C `traceparent` header in message attributes).
- **One more system to run.** The broker itself must be highly available, monitored and capacity-planned.

> [!tip] Async request-reply
> Sometimes you need a result but the work is slow (video transcoding, report generation). Return `202 Accepted` with a job ID, process via a queue, and let the client poll a status endpoint or receive a webhook. Webhooks and WebSockets are covered in the API design module.

## Key takeaways

- Keep work required for the immediate success response on that response path.
- Slow jobs can return a job ID with 202 Accepted, then expose status or notify the client.
- Asynchronous writes require an explicit pending-state experience; message trace context connects the request to later work.

## Further reading

- [Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling)
- [Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library)](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/)
- [Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/)

questions.prompt: You are designing an e-commerce checkout whose immediate success response requires payment authorisation and whose loyalty points may appear later. Which of these steps are good candidates to move **off** the synchronous request path and onto a queue? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sending the order confirmation email
options.explanation: Correct. The user does not need the email to arrive before the page loads, and email providers are slow and occasionally unavailable. A queue with retries is a natural fit.

options.text: Authorising the card payment
options.explanation: Wrong. The user needs to know immediately whether the payment succeeded before you can show 'order placed'. This is the classic case where synchronous communication is the right choice.

options.text: Updating the recommendation model with the purchase
options.explanation: Correct. Recommendations can lag by seconds or minutes without harming the user, and the ML pipeline should not be able to slow down or fail checkout.

options.text: Awarding loyalty points
options.explanation: Correct. Points can be applied eventually. The UI can say 'points will appear shortly', and failures can be retried from the queue rather than failing the purchase.

options.text: Checking the basket total against the price the user saw
options.explanation: Wrong. This is a validation that must pass **before** you charge the customer, so it belongs on the synchronous path. Doing it later would mean charging the wrong amount and fixing it afterwards.

questions.workedExample:
Ask one question of each step: **does the user's immediate response depend on the result?**

| Step | Needed for response? | Placement |
|---|---|---|
| Price check | Yes, before charging | Sync |
| Card auth | Yes, shows success | Sync |
| Email | No | Async |
| Recommendations | No | Async |
| Loyalty points | No | Async |

The pattern is **sync at the edge, async inside**: validate and charge synchronously, write the order, publish `OrderPlaced`, and let everything else react to that event.

questions.prompt: A reporting endpoint takes 2–8 minutes to build a spreadsheet. Clients currently hold an HTTP connection open and frequently hit the load balancer's 60-second idle timeout. What is the most robust redesign?

options.text: Raise the load balancer idle timeout to 10 minutes
options.explanation: Wrong. This papers over the problem. Long-held connections tie up server resources, may encounter intermediary timeouts. Without durable job identity and idempotent submission, disconnects can lose access to results and retries can duplicate work.

options.text: Have the client retry the request automatically whenever it times out
options.explanation: Wrong. Each retry starts another 2–8 minute job while the first may still be running, multiplying load. Without idempotency it can also produce duplicate reports.

options.text: Return 202 Accepted with a job ID, enqueue the work, and let the client poll a status URL or receive a callback
options.explanation: Correct. This is asynchronous request-reply. The request can be acknowledged after durable acceptance, the work is load-levelled by a queue, and the result survives client disconnects because it is stored against the job ID.

options.text: Run the report on a bigger server so it finishes inside 60 seconds
options.explanation: Wrong. Vertical scaling may help a little but will not reliably cut an 8-minute job below 60 seconds, and the problem returns as data grows. It also leaves bursts of requests able to overload the service.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Identify the mismatch**: the work takes minutes, but the existing request path has timeouts shorter than the job duration.
2. **Split acceptance from completion**: `POST /reports` validates the request, atomically records a job (`status = PENDING`) and an outbox entry for `{jobId}`, then returns `202 Accepted` with `Location: /reports/{jobId}`.
3. **Process asynchronously**: an outbox relay publishes committed outbox entries; workers pull from the queue, build the file, upload it to object storage and set `status = DONE`.
4. **Deliver the result**: the client polls `GET /reports/{jobId}` (with a `Retry-After` hint) or registers a webhook.
5. **Failure behaviour**: after durable acceptance, the job survives client disconnects; a retry uses the same idempotency key. Worker crashes can trigger redelivery within retention limits, so processing and completion updates must tolerate duplicates.

Webhooks themselves are covered in the API design module.

questions.prompt: A settings page used to save notification preferences synchronously. To "improve resilience", a team changed it to publish `PreferencesChanged` to a queue and return `200 OK` at once; a worker writes the database a few hundred milliseconds later. Users now report that after saving, the page reloads and shows their **old** settings. What is the best response?

options.text: Add more workers so the queue is drained faster
options.explanation: Wrong. More workers shrink the window but cannot remove it: there is always some delay between the response and the write, and under load or during a worker outage it grows to seconds or minutes.

options.text: Switch the queue to FIFO
options.explanation: Wrong. FIFO controls the order messages are processed in, not when. The reload can still happen before the worker has written anything.

options.text: Have the client wait one second before reloading
options.explanation: Wrong. A fixed sleep is slow for everyone and still wrong whenever the backlog exceeds one second. It hides the design problem rather than fixing it.

options.text: Write the preferences synchronously, because the user needs to read their own write, then publish an event for other systems that react to it
options.explanation: Correct. The user is waiting for this answer and immediately reads it back, which is the case where synchronous is right. Systems that merely react to the change, such as an email digest, can still consume an event published afterwards (ideally via an outbox).

questions.workedExample:
1. Apply the lesson's question: **does the user need the result now?** Here, yes. They save and immediately read back.
2. "Strong read-after-write needed" is in the *Sync* column of the decision table.
3. The async version returns before the write exists, so a reload races the worker.
4. Better split:
   - Sync: validate and commit the preferences row, return the saved state, and route immediate reads to an authority that includes that commit.
   - Async: publish `PreferencesChanged` for search, analytics or notification services.
5. Resilience still improves where it matters: the downstream consumers are decoupled, while the user-facing path stays correct.

questions.prompt: Your distributed traces show the checkout request ending at the moment it publishes `OrderPlaced` to a queue. The email worker's spans appear as separate, unconnected traces, so support cannot follow one order from click to confirmation email. What fixes this?

options.text: Propagate the trace context (for example a W3C `traceparent` value) in the message attributes, and have consumers continue the trace from it
options.explanation: Correct. Tracing links spans through a shared trace ID passed along with each request. Over HTTP that travels in a header; over a broker it must travel in the message, and consumer instrumentation uses a parent relationship or span links as appropriate, especially for batched or multiple-message processing.

options.text: Make the email call synchronous so it appears in the checkout trace
options.explanation: Wrong. This sacrifices the benefits of async (checkout now waits for email) just to fix observability. Context propagation solves the tracing gap without changing the architecture.

options.text: Record 100% of traces instead of a sample
options.explanation: Wrong. Sampling decides how many traces are recorded, not whether spans in different processes are linked. Two unconnected traces sampled at 100% are still unconnected.

options.text: Log the queue name in every service
options.explanation: Wrong. The queue name is the same for every order, so it cannot link one order's spans together. You need an identifier unique to the request, carried across the hop.

questions.workedExample:
1. A trace is held together by a **trace ID** that each hop passes to the next.
2. Instrumented HTTP clients and servers can propagate it in headers such as `traceparent`.
3. A message broker is a hop too, but the trace context only crosses it if you put it **in the message**: SQS message attributes, Kafka record headers, AMQP headers.
4. The consumer extracts it and connects processing using a parent relationship or span links according to the instrumentation conventions.
5. Check the specific producer and consumer instrumentation for supported propagation and span relationships; do not assume propagation is automatic.

lessons.title: Competing consumers and acknowledgement failures
lessons.summary: Trace receive, process and acknowledgement to see why a worker crash can cause loss or duplication.
lessons.body:
A message queue is the simplest broker: producers put messages in, consumers take them out, and **each delivery is assigned to one competing consumer, rather than broadcast to every consumer**. This is called **point-to-point messaging**. It is the workhorse behind background jobs, email sending, image processing and most "do this later" tasks.

## Competing consumers

You scale a queue by running several consumers against it. They **compete** for messages: whichever is free takes the next one.

```
           ┌──▶ worker A
producer ─▶[ m5 m4 m3 m2 m1 ]──▶ worker B
           └──▶ worker C
```

This gives you three properties almost for free:

- **Horizontal scaling.** More workers can increase throughput until queue partitions, broker resources, contention or downstream capacity limit it.
- **Resilience.** If worker B crashes, A and C keep going.
- **Natural load balancing.** A fast worker simply asks for more often.

The catch is **ordering**. With several competing consumers, m2 may finish before m1. If ordering matters, you need FIFO queues with group IDs (covered later in this module) or partitioned processing on a log like Kafka; application concurrency must also preserve the required order.

## The core problem: when is a message "done"?

A consumer can crash halfway through processing. If the broker deleted the message the moment it was handed out, that work would be lost. So brokers separate **delivery** from **completion** using **acknowledgements**.

```
1. receive   broker ──m1──▶ worker
2. process   worker does the work
3. ack       worker ──ack──▶ broker
4. delete    broker removes m1
```

If step 3 never happens, the broker assumes the worker died and **redelivers** the message to someone else. This is what makes queues reliable, and it is also why messages can be **delivered more than once**: a worker might finish step 2, then crash before step 3.

> [!warning] Ack after, not before
> Acknowledging before processing (auto-ack) gives you *at-most-once* delivery: a crash mid-processing loses the message. Acknowledging after processing gives you *at-least-once*: a crash after processing but before the ack means a duplicate. Most systems choose at-least-once and make consumers idempotent.

## Key takeaways

- Consumers share work rather than each receiving a broadcast copy.
- Completion acknowledgements let the broker redeliver unfinished work after a consumer disappears.
- A crash after an effect but before acknowledgement can repeat the effect; consumers must tolerate duplicates.

## Further reading

- [RabbitMQ tutorial: work queues, acks and fair dispatch](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-two-python)
- [Competing Consumers pattern (Azure Architecture Center)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/competing-consumers)

questions.prompt: Three workers consume from the same SQS standard queue. A producer sends one message. In normal operation, how many workers process it?

options.text: All three, because each worker is subscribed to the queue
options.explanation: Wrong. That is publish/subscribe behaviour. A point-to-point queue hands each message to one consumer; to get a copy per consumer you would need a topic (such as SNS) feeding a queue each.

options.text: Exactly one, and it is guaranteed never to be delivered again
options.explanation: Wrong. Normally one worker gets it, but SQS standard queues are at-least-once: a visibility timeout expiring or a rare duplicate means the message can be delivered again. 'Never again' is too strong.

options.text: One of them, usually exactly once, with occasional redelivery possible
options.explanation: Correct. Workers compete for messages and SQS hides a received message from the others. Under failures or timeouts it can be redelivered, which is why consumers should be idempotent.

options.text: None until all three acknowledge readiness
options.explanation: Wrong. There is no group readiness handshake in a queue. Any worker that calls ReceiveMessage can take the next available message.

questions.workedExample:
1. A queue is a **point-to-point** channel: one message, one consumer.
2. When worker A calls `ReceiveMessage`, SQS returns the message and makes it **invisible** to B and C.
3. A processes it and calls `DeleteMessage`. Done; B and C never see it.
4. Edge case: if A does not delete it before the visibility timeout ends, it becomes visible and B or C may receive it.
5. Separately, standard queues may occasionally deliver a duplicate even without a timeout.

So the honest answer is "one, at least once".

questions.prompt: A RabbitMQ consumer receives a message with **manual acknowledgements** enabled, starts processing, and its process is killed before it sends `basic.ack`. Assume it has not expired or reached a delivery limit. What happens to the message?

options.text: It is requeued when the channel closes and delivered to another consumer
options.explanation: Correct. RabbitMQ tracks unacknowledged deliveries per channel. When the connection drops, those messages go back to the queue and are redelivered with the `redelivered` flag set.

options.text: It is lost, because it was already delivered
options.explanation: Wrong. That would happen with auto-ack, where the broker considers the message done as soon as it is sent. With manual acks the broker keeps it until it is acknowledged.

options.text: It moves straight to the dead-letter exchange
options.explanation: Wrong. Dead-lettering happens on reject/nack without requeue, TTL expiry, length limits or exceeding a quorum queue's delivery limit. A single consumer crash simply requeues the message.

options.text: It stays invisible until a 30-second visibility timeout expires
options.explanation: Wrong. Visibility timeouts are how SQS works, because SQS has no persistent connection. RabbitMQ detects the dead consumer directly through the closed connection.

questions.workedExample:
1. With manual acks, RabbitMQ marks the delivery as **unacked** and keeps the message.
2. The process dies, so its TCP connection closes (or, if the machine vanished without closing it, the heartbeat times out, typically within a minute or two with the default 60-second heartbeat timeout).
3. RabbitMQ sees the channel close and returns every unacked message on it to the queue.
4. Another consumer gets it with `redelivered=true`. A careful consumer can use that flag as a hint to check for duplicate work.

Contrast: in SQS the equivalent safety net is the visibility timeout.

lessons.title: SQS visibility timeouts and processing leases
lessons.summary: Tune visibility for job duration and understand why receipt handles and timeouts do not guarantee exclusive work.
lessons.body:
SQS treats a received message as temporarily leased work. A worker must finish and delete it before that lease expires, or extend the lease while it continues.

## How SQS does it: visibility timeouts

Amazon SQS has no persistent connection between broker and consumer, so it cannot notice that a consumer died. Instead it uses a **visibility timeout**.

1. A consumer calls `ReceiveMessage`. SQS returns the message plus a **receipt handle**, and normally hides it from other consumers. Standard queues can still deliver duplicates during the visibility window, so visibility is not an exclusive-processing lock.
2. The message stays invisible for the visibility timeout (default **30 seconds**, maximum **12 hours**).
3. The consumer uses the most recent receipt handle with DeleteMessage after processing. Standard queues can occasionally redeliver even after deletion, and an obsolete receipt handle does not guarantee deletion.
4. If not, the message becomes visible again and another consumer can receive it.

```
0 s     receive m1 (invisible)
0–30 s  worker processing...
30 s    timeout: m1 visible again
31 s    worker B receives m1 (dup!)
```

(Times are seconds after the first receive.)

The key tuning rule: **set the visibility timeout comfortably longer than your worst-case processing time.** Too short, and slow jobs reappear and are done twice. Too long, and a message whose worker really did crash sits hidden for the whole timeout before anyone retries it.

When SQS triggers AWS Lambda, AWS recommends a visibility timeout of at least **six times the function's timeout**, plus any batching window (`MaximumBatchingWindowInSeconds`). A function with a 2-minute timeout therefore wants at least 12 minutes. The margin exists because Lambda may need to retry a batch if the function is throttled, and all of that must happen before the messages reappear. Lambda refuses outright to connect a function whose timeout exceeds the queue's visibility timeout.

If jobs genuinely vary (a 10-second job sometimes takes 10 minutes), the worker can call `ChangeMessageVisibility` periodically as a heartbeat to extend its lease. That keeps a short timeout, so crashed work is retried quickly, without timing out healthy slow jobs. Extensions cannot take one receive beyond the 12-hour maximum: extending does not reset that limit.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a meeting room booked in 30-minute slots
> You book a meeting room for 30 minutes. If you overrun without extending the booking, the next person is allowed to walk in, and now two meetings are happening in one room. If you finish early, you release the room so someone else can use it straight away.
>
> **How it maps:** Receiving a message is taking the booking; the visibility timeout is the slot length. Overrunning is a job that takes longer than the timeout, so a second worker receives it. Extending the booking is `ChangeMessageVisibility`, and releasing the room is `DeleteMessage`.
>
> **Where it stops:** A booking system normally never double-books an active slot, but an SQS standard queue can occasionally deliver a duplicate even inside the visibility window, so the lease is not an exclusive lock. And SQS never checks whether you are still "in the room": only a delete, an extension or the timeout changes anything.

## Key takeaways

- Visibility temporarily hides a delivery; SQS standard queues can still deliver a duplicate.
- Delete with the latest receipt handle after successful processing, and extend visibility when long jobs need it.
- For SQS-triggered Lambda, AWS recommends at least six times the function timeout plus the batching window.

## Further reading

- [Amazon SQS visibility timeout (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html)
- [SQS event source configuration (AWS Lambda)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-configure.html)

questions.prompt: Your SQS consumer resizes videos. The queue's visibility timeout is the default 30 seconds, and jobs take between 20 and 90 seconds. Users complain about receiving some processed videos twice and the worker fleet seems busier than expected. What is going on, and what is the best fix?

options.text: SQS standard queues randomly duplicate messages; switch to a FIFO queue
options.explanation: Wrong. Standard queues can occasionally duplicate, but that is rare. Here the cause is systematic: every job longer than 30 seconds reappears. FIFO deduplication only covers producer-side duplicates within 5 minutes and would not stop visibility-timeout redelivery.

options.text: Workers are deleting messages too early; they should delete before starting work
options.explanation: Wrong. Deleting before processing would stop duplicates but lose the job whenever a worker crashes mid-way. That swaps at-least-once for at-most-once, which is a bad trade for paid video processing.

options.text: Jobs longer than 30 seconds become visible again and are picked up by a second worker; raise the timeout above the worst case or extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility while working
options.explanation: Correct. A job over 30 seconds can be redelivered while the first worker is still running, so two workers do the same work and both publish a result. A timeout of several minutes, or a heartbeat that extends the lease, reduces timeout-driven duplicates, but does not eliminate all redelivery.

options.text: Long polling is causing workers to receive the same message
options.explanation: Wrong. Long polling only controls how long ReceiveMessage waits for a message to arrive. It does not make an invisible message visible to other consumers.

questions.workedExample:
Trace a 60-second job (times in seconds after the first receive):

```
0 s   worker A receives m (hidden)
30 s  timeout expires, m visible
31 s  worker B receives m
60 s  A finishes, tries delete with old
      handle (deletion not guaranteed)
91 s  B finishes: second result
```

1. Every job over 30 s becomes eligible for redelivery, and some 90 s jobs could even be picked up three times.
2. Fleet utilisation rises because the same work is done repeatedly.
3. Fix options:
   - Set the timeout to comfortably exceed the worst case, for example 5 minutes.
   - Or keep it short and have the worker call `ChangeMessageVisibility` every ~20 s as a heartbeat. This keeps fast failover if a worker dies.
4. Still make the consumer idempotent (for example, key the output on the job ID), because at-least-once delivery remains.

questions.prompt: An SQS queue triggers an AWS Lambda function whose timeout is 2 minutes. The queue's visibility timeout is also 2 minutes, which Lambda accepted. During a traffic spike the function is throttled, and afterwards the team finds some orders processed twice and others in the dead-letter queue although the code never failed on them. What is the best diagnosis?

options.text: SQS standard queues randomly duplicate messages under load; switching to FIFO would fix both symptoms
options.explanation: Wrong. Standard queues can occasionally duplicate, but that does not explain healthy messages reaching the dead-letter queue. The pattern points to messages reappearing while Lambda was still retrying the throttled batches.

options.text: The function timeout is too long; cut it to 30 seconds so batches finish before visibility expires
options.explanation: Wrong. A shorter function timeout would make slow but healthy batches fail. The problem is that the queue gives no spare time for Lambda's throttling retries, not that the function is allowed too long.

options.text: Visibility equal to the function timeout leaves no room for throttling retries, so messages reappear, are received again and count towards maxReceiveCount; raise visibility to at least six times the function timeout
options.explanation: Correct. The visibility clock starts when the batch is received. If Lambda has to retry a throttled invocation, the messages can become visible again and be received a second time (duplicates), and each receive counts towards the redrive policy's limit (healthy messages in the DLQ). AWS recommends at least six times the function timeout, plus any batching window, here at least 12 minutes.

options.text: The dead-letter queue is misconfigured; delete it so that messages are retried forever
options.explanation: Wrong. Removing the DLQ would hide the symptom and let genuine poison messages loop indefinitely. The cause is the visibility timeout, and AWS also recommends a maxReceiveCount of at least 5 so throttling alone does not dead-letter messages.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start from the clue that *healthy* messages were dead-lettered and some were processed twice. Both are what happens when messages become visible again while their first attempt is still in progress.
2. The visibility clock starts when Lambda's poller receives the batch. If the function is throttled, Lambda retries the invocation, and that waiting time also runs against the 2-minute visibility timeout.
3. Once the timeout passes, the messages reappear. A second poller receives them (duplicate processing), and each receive increments the receive count. Reach `maxReceiveCount` and SQS moves a message to the DLQ even though the code never failed on it.
4. Fix: follow AWS's guidance of a visibility timeout of at least **six times the function timeout**, plus any batching window, so at least 12 minutes here. Set `maxReceiveCount` to at least 5 so throttling alone does not dead-letter messages.
5. Keep the consumer idempotent, because at-least-once delivery still allows occasional duplicates.

lessons.title: SQS polling, payloads and FIFO throughput
lessons.summary: Reduce empty receives, keep large payloads outside the queue and size FIFO traffic by message groups.
lessons.body:
Once acknowledgement timing is correct, the remaining SQS design choices are how to fetch efficiently, what belongs in the payload, and how ordered traffic is distributed.

## SQS limits, polling and FIFO throughput

Other SQS details worth knowing (quotas as of 2026):

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Max message size | 1 MiB (256 KB before 2025) |
| Retention | 1 min–14 days (default 4) |
| Long poll wait | up to 20 s |
| Batch receive | up to 10 messages |

For anything bigger than the limit (images, large documents), use the **claim check** pattern: store the payload in S3 and send a small message holding its key. AWS's extended client libraries do this for you.

Use **long polling** (`WaitTimeSeconds=20`). Short polling returns immediately even when the queue is empty, which wastes requests (and money, since SQS bills per request) and can miss messages because it samples only a subset of servers.

Standard SQS queues offer nearly unlimited throughput but only **best-effort ordering** and **at-least-once** delivery. **SQS FIFO queues** guarantee order within a *message group* and deduplicate within a 5-minute window, at lower throughput. Without high-throughput mode, a FIFO queue handles 300 API calls per second per action (`SendMessage`, `ReceiveMessage`, `DeleteMessage`). Each call can carry a batch of up to 10 messages, so batching is what lifts the ceiling from 300 to about 3,000 messages per second per action. If a FIFO producer throttles at exactly 300 or 3,000 messages a second, that limit is the first suspect.

**High-throughput mode** spreads message groups across internal partitions and raises the limit to thousands or tens of thousands of calls per second, depending on the region (as of 2026). SQS hashes each message group ID to choose a partition, so the extra capacity only appears if you use many distinct message group IDs. Every message in one group still lands on one partition, because the group's order must be kept.

## Key takeaways

- Long polling reduces empty receive traffic; batches move up to ten messages per SQS API call.
- Use a claim check for large files: store the object and send its reference.
- FIFO orders each message group; high throughput also requires enough distinct groups to distribute load.

## Further reading

- [Amazon SQS message quotas (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/quotas-messages.html)

questions.prompt: Idle SQS consumers repeatedly call ReceiveMessage with short polling. Most responses contain no messages, and empty receives dominate the request bill. Which change most directly addresses this?

options.text: No change: empty receives are free
options.explanation: Wrong. Empty receive requests are still billed.

options.text: Increase only the requested batch size
options.explanation: Wrong. Batching helps when messages are available; it does not make an empty short poll wait.

options.text: Use long polling so an idle receive can wait for work
options.explanation: Correct. Fewer empty calls are needed while the queue is quiet, and a request can return when work becomes available.

options.text: Keep short polling but delete messages in batches
options.explanation: Wrong. Batch deletion can save delete requests, but it does not address idle receive traffic.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify what is expensive: repeated empty API requests, not message processing.
2. Long polling lets a receive wait up to its configured duration instead of returning immediately when no message is found.
3. Configure WaitTimeSeconds, commonly 20 seconds, and make the HTTP timeout long enough for that wait.
4. Batch receives and deletes complement this when traffic is available. Actual savings depend on traffic and polling behaviour.

questions.prompt: Users upload scanned contracts of up to 20 MB. The API base64-encodes each PDF and sends it in an SQS message to an OCR worker. Sends for larger files fail. What is the best design?

options.text: Split each PDF into 1 MiB chunks across several messages and reassemble them in the worker
options.explanation: Wrong. Competing consumers would receive chunks of the same file on different workers, in any order, and a single lost or dead-lettered chunk breaks the whole file. You would be rebuilding a file transfer protocol on top of a queue.

options.text: Compress the PDF before base64-encoding it
options.explanation: Wrong. Many scanned PDFs already contain compressed image data, and base64 adds about a third. Compression cannot reliably guarantee every allowed 20 MB file fits under the 1 MiB message limit.

options.text: Upload the PDF to S3 and send a small message containing the bucket and key
options.explanation: Correct. This is the claim check pattern. The queue carries a small reference and the large payload lives in object storage. AWS's extended client libraries for SQS automate it.

options.text: Switch to an SQS FIFO queue, which allows larger messages
options.explanation: Wrong. FIFO queues have the same maximum message size as standard queues. FIFO changes ordering and deduplication, not payload limits.

questions.workedExample:
1. Check the limit: an SQS message can be at most **1 MiB** (it was 256 KB until 2025), and FIFO queues have the same limit.
2. Estimate the payload. Base64 writes every 3 bytes of binary as 4 text characters, so it makes data about a third bigger: a 20 MB PDF becomes roughly 27 MB of message body, far over the limit. Compression cannot reliably close a gap that large for already-compressed scans.
3. Claim check:
   - `PUT s3://contracts/in/abc.pdf`
   - send `{"bucket":"contracts", "key":"in/abc.pdf"}`
   - the worker downloads and processes an immutable object version; retain it until retries and DLQ redrive can no longer need it.
4. Bonus: messages stay small, so receives are cheap and fast, and the S3 object can have its own lifecycle and encryption policy.
5. Make the worker idempotent on a unique job ID and immutable object version (a reused object key alone is insufficient), since the message is still delivered at least once.

questions.prompt: An order pipeline in eu-west-1 must sustain **6,000 messages per second** through an SQS FIFO queue, ordered per customer. Producers send batches of 10 with `MessageGroupId = "orders"` on every message, using default queue settings. Sends throttle at about 3,000 messages per second. What change is needed?

options.text: Switch to a standard queue, which has nearly unlimited throughput
options.explanation: Wrong. A standard queue would meet the throughput but gives only best-effort ordering, breaking the per-customer ordering requirement.

options.text: Enable high-throughput mode and set `MessageGroupId` to the customer ID
options.explanation: Correct. High-throughput mode raises the per-action limit, but SQS scales it by spreading message groups across partitions. With a single group everything stays on one partition; with one group per customer the load spreads and per-customer order is kept.

options.text: Increase the batch size to 20 messages per call
options.explanation: Wrong. SQS batch calls are capped at 10 messages. The 3,000 figure is exactly 300 calls per second × 10 messages.

options.text: Enable high-throughput mode and keep the single message group
options.explanation: Wrong. Messages in one group must be kept in order, so they map to one partition and are limited to that partition's throughput. SQS may return several group messages in one batch; the application must apply their effects in the required order.

questions.workedExample:
1. Diagnose the 3,000 ceiling. A FIFO queue in default mode allows 300 calls per second per action, and a batch call carries at most 10 messages. 300 calls × 10 messages is 3,000 messages a second, exactly where the producers throttle. A bigger batch is not allowed.
2. High-throughput mode raises the limit (up to tens of thousands of calls per second in the largest regions, as of 2026), but only by spreading **message groups** across partitions. SQS hashes the group ID to pick a partition.
3. A constant group ID means one group mapped to one partition, so the extra capacity never appears. It also imposes a global ordering requirement nobody actually has.
4. The real requirement is **per customer**, so `MessageGroupId = customerId`.
5. Now thousands of groups spread across partitions, and many consumers can work in parallel on different customers while each customer's messages stay in order.

lessons.title: RabbitMQ prefetch and replicated quorum queues
lessons.summary: Control unacknowledged deliveries with prefetch and predict how many replica failures a quorum queue survives.
lessons.body:
RabbitMQ pushes deliveries over an existing connection. The consumer controls its exposure with prefetch, while replicated quorum queues protect the broker-side record of the work.

## How RabbitMQ does it: channels, acks and prefetch

RabbitMQ consumers hold a long-lived TCP connection. The broker *pushes* messages to them, and it knows a consumer has died when the connection or its AMQP channel closes.

- Consumers send `basic.ack` when done, or `basic.nack` / `basic.reject` to give up (optionally with `requeue=true`).
- Unacknowledged messages on a closed channel are **requeued** automatically.
- **Consumer prefetch** (`basic.qos`) limits how many unacknowledged messages a consumer may hold at once.

The prefetch limit is a crucial knob. A prefetch of 0 means unlimited: with a classic queue, the first consumer to connect can be pushed a large share of the backlog as unacknowledged deliveries, leaving little for consumers that join later. (Quorum queues cap prefetch at 2,000, and broker defaults can impose other bounds.) A prefetch of 1 prevents a consumer holding more than one unacknowledged delivery, but it significantly reduces throughput because each consumer waits a network round trip between messages. RabbitMQ's documentation says values from about 100 to 300 usually give near-optimal throughput; lower values share slow jobs more evenly. Measure with your real processing times.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: markers sharing a pile of exam scripts
> A pile of exam scripts sits on a table. If there is no rule, the first marker to arrive can take most of the pile back to their desk, and markers who arrive later find almost nothing left. Say "take at most 50 at a time" and everyone gets a share, while each marker still has enough on their desk not to keep walking back to the table.
>
> **How it maps:** The pile is the queue, each marker is a consumer, and the scripts on a desk are unacknowledged deliveries. The "at most 50" rule is the prefetch limit: small enough to share work fairly, large enough to avoid a round trip per message.
>
> **Where it stops:** A marker can hand scripts back whenever they like, but RabbitMQ only returns unacknowledged deliveries to the queue when the consumer rejects them or its channel closes. And RabbitMQ pushes scripts to the desk; consumers do not walk over and fetch them.

Producers publish to a **RabbitMQ exchange**, which routes each message into queues. There are four exchange types: direct exchange, topic exchange, fanout exchange and headers exchange. For durability use **quorum queues**, which replicate each queue across nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm. A write is confirmed once a majority of replicas have it, and the queue keeps working only while a majority is still up. So a 3-replica queue survives one node failure and a 5-replica queue survives two.

```formula reference
f = ⌊(n − 1) / 2⌋
where
f: the number of replicas (nodes) that can fail while the queue still accepts and confirms writes
n: the number of replicas of the queue, usually an odd number such as 3 or 5
⌊ ⌋: floor: round down to the whole number below, so ⌊1.5⌋ = 1
In words: a majority must survive, so a queue can lose just under half its replicas: 3 replicas survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2, and a fourth replica adds no extra tolerance over 3.
```

A 4-replica queue still survives only one failure, because 2 out of 4 is not a majority; that is why replica counts are usually odd. Lose the majority and the queue stops accepting work rather than risk losing confirmed messages. Quorum queues are always durable and cannot be exclusive or transient.

The older alternative, *classic mirrored queues*, was deprecated for years and **removed in RabbitMQ 4.0** (2024). Anything still relying on mirroring must move to quorum queues (or streams) before upgrading.

## Key takeaways

- RabbitMQ requeues unacknowledged deliveries when their channel closes.
- Prefetch limits in-flight work and can prevent an early consumer taking a large backlog; benchmark the setting.
- Quorum queues need a surviving majority, and classic mirroring was removed in RabbitMQ 4.0.

## Further reading

- [RabbitMQ tutorial: work queues, acks and fair dispatch](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-two-python)
- [Quorum queues (RabbitMQ docs)](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues)

questions.prompt: A RabbitMQ classic queue using manual acknowledgements holds 50,000 messages. You start one consumer with **no prefetch limit**, then 30 seconds later start nine more. The nine new consumers sit idle while the first one is overwhelmed. Why?

options.text: RabbitMQ only allows one consumer per queue at a time
options.explanation: Wrong. RabbitMQ supports many consumers per queue and round-robins deliveries among them. (Single active consumer is an opt-in feature, not the default.)

options.text: The queue is a FIFO queue, so ordering forces a single consumer
options.explanation: Wrong. RabbitMQ queues are FIFO by nature but still distribute messages to multiple consumers. Ordering across consumers is lost, but distribution still happens.

options.text: The new consumers need to use basic.get polling instead
options.explanation: Wrong. Polling with basic.get is less efficient and would not reclaim the messages already pushed to the first consumer. The fix is to limit unacked messages per consumer.

options.text: The first consumer was pushed almost every message as unacked deliveries, so there is little left in the queue for the others
options.explanation: Correct. With unlimited prefetch, RabbitMQ pushes messages as fast as the network allows. The first consumer buffers tens of thousands of unacked messages, and the new consumers only get what arrives afterwards.

questions.workedExample:
1. RabbitMQ pushes messages to consumers. In this explicitly unlimited classic-queue configuration, there is no prefetch cap. Broker default prefetch settings and quorum-queue limits can differ.
2. In 30 seconds, the first consumer can be sent most of the 50,000 messages, which sit in its client buffer.
3. Those messages remain retained as unacknowledged deliveries but are not ready for assignment to other consumers, so new consumers see an almost empty queue.
4. Fix: set prefetch, for example `basic.qos(prefetch_count=50)`. Now each consumer holds at most 50 unacked messages and the rest stay in the queue to be shared.
5. Choosing the value: if processing takes 20 ms and the network round trip is 2 ms, even a prefetch of 10 keeps a consumer busy; larger values may add buffering with little benefit in this example; measure with the actual workload.
