lessons.title: Poison messages, receive counts and dead letters
lessons.summary: Classify failures, set aside broken messages and keep recoverable outages from exhausting the retry budget.
lessons.body:
After processing fails, decide whether another attempt can help. A durable queue gives you time to recover, but repeated receives alone do not repair malformed input or an unavailable dependency.

## Poison messages and dead-letter queues

Some messages will never succeed: malformed JSON, a reference to a deleted customer, a bug triggered by one specific input. Without protection, such a **poison message** is retried forever, wasting capacity and, in FIFO queues, blocking later work in its message group when processing preserves order.

The fix is a **dead-letter queue (DLQ)**: after a set number of failed attempts (say 5), move the message aside.

```
main queue ──fail×5──▶ DLQ
    │                   │
    ▼                   ▼
 workers           alert + inspect
```

- **SQS**: set a *redrive policy* with `maxReceiveCount` (say 5). SQS tracks `ApproximateReceiveCount`; when it exceeds the limit, the message moves to the DLQ. You can later *redrive* messages back to the source queue once the bug is fixed.
- **RabbitMQ**: configure a *dead-letter exchange*. Messages are dead-lettered when rejected without requeue, when their TTL expires, or when the queue exceeds its length limit. Quorum queues also enforce a `delivery-limit`, which **defaults to 20 since RabbitMQ 4.0**: a message redelivered more often than that is dead-lettered if a dead-letter exchange is configured, and **dropped** if not. Exactly which kinds of return count towards the limit has changed between 4.x releases, so check the docs for your version.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: the post office's dead letter office
> When a letter cannot be delivered after a few tries, the post office does not keep sending the van out with it forever. It moves the letter to a separate office where someone opens it, works out what went wrong and decides whether it can be sent on.
>
> **How it maps:** The repeated delivery attempts are redeliveries counted against `maxReceiveCount` or `delivery-limit`. The dead letter office is the DLQ: a holding area that stops one broken message wasting capacity, and a place where a person investigates before redriving it.
>
> **Where it stops:** A failed letter has had no effect, but a message can reach the DLQ after its side effect already happened and only the acknowledgement was lost. A DLQ also deletes messages when its retention period ends, and nothing reaches it unless you configure one.

> [!tip] A DLQ nobody watches is a black hole
> Always alarm when DLQ depth is above zero, keep DLQ retention longer than the source queue's (otherwise messages can expire before anyone looks), and record *why* a message failed (an error attribute or a log line with the message ID).

## Choosing a receive count

Too low a `maxReceiveCount` (1 or 2) dead-letters messages that hit a transient error, such as a database failover lasting 20 seconds. Too high (100) lets a poison message burn capacity for ages. Three to ten is an illustrative starting range to test against expected outage duration and retry cost, combined with **backoff** between attempts so that transient faults have time to clear.

SQS standard queues have no native per-message backoff, but you can approximate it by calling `ChangeMessageVisibility` on failure with an increasing delay (for example, 30 s, 2 min, 10 min based on the receive count).

## Queue vs log, in one table

| | Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) | Log (Kafka) |
|---|---|---|
| After ack | Deleted | Retained |
| Unit of scaling | Message | Partition |
| Replay | No | Yes |
| Per-message retry | Easy | Awkward |

Queues shine for **task distribution**: independent jobs where each should be done once and individual failures should be retried or set aside. Logs, covered later, shine for **event streams** that many consumers read and replay.

## Key takeaways

- A poison message needs a bounded retry path and an inspected DLQ, rather than endless redelivery.
- Receive limits and visibility delays must accommodate the outages you expect to recover from.
- RabbitMQ quorum delivery limits can drop messages without a dead-letter exchange; SQS FIFO poison work can block its group.
- Queues suit individually retried tasks; retained logs suit replayable streams.

## Further reading

- [Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)
- [Quorum queues (RabbitMQ docs)](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues)
- [Dead Letter Channel (Enterprise Integration Patterns)](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/DeadLetterChannel.html)

questions.prompt: You are adding a dead-letter queue to an SQS-based order pipeline. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Alarm whenever the DLQ's visible message count is above zero
options.explanation: Correct. Every message in the DLQ needs investigation; an effect may already have committed before its acknowledgement was lost. A non-zero count needs a human, so it should page or at least notify someone.

options.text: Give the DLQ a longer retention period than the source queue
options.explanation: Correct. In SQS standard queues, a message's age is counted from when it was originally enqueued, so a short DLQ retention can delete it soon after it arrives. AWS recommends a longer DLQ retention.

options.text: Set maxReceiveCount to 1 so failures are surfaced immediately
options.explanation: Wrong. One failure is often a transient error such as a database failover or throttling. Dead-lettering on the first attempt sends recoverable messages aside and creates manual work.

options.text: Record the failure reason (error and stack trace) alongside the message ID in logs
options.explanation: Correct. When someone inspects the DLQ, knowing why each message failed is what lets them fix the bug and redrive confidently rather than guessing.

options.text: Automatically redrive DLQ messages back to the source queue every minute
options.explanation: Wrong. That recreates the infinite retry loop the DLQ was meant to break. Redrive deliberately, after fixing the cause.

questions.workedExample:
Think about what a DLQ is for: it is a **holding area for messages that need human attention**.

1. Humans must find out: alarm on depth > 0.
2. Messages must still be there when they look: longer retention (SQS allows up to 14 days).
3. Humans need context: log the error with the message ID.
4. Transient failures should not land there: use a `maxReceiveCount` of roughly 3–10 with backoff.
5. Redrive is a deliberate act after a fix, using the SQS redrive feature, not a timer.

questions.prompt: An SQS consumer writes orders to Postgres. The queue has a 30-second visibility timeout and `maxReceiveCount = 3`. On failure the consumer does nothing; assume prompt polling as each timeout ends and ignore duplicate receives. A database failover makes every write fail for **2 minutes**. What happens to messages received at the start of the outage, and what is the best improvement?

options.text: They are retried until the database returns, then succeed; no change needed
options.explanation: Wrong. With a 30-second timeout and 3 receives, the attempts happen at about 0, 30 and 60 seconds. All three fail inside the 2-minute outage and the message is moved to the DLQ before the database returns.

options.text: They are dead-lettered after about 90 seconds; add increasing backoff using ChangeMessageVisibility so retries span the outage
options.explanation: Correct. Receives at 0 s, 30 s and 60 s all fail; on the next receive (about 90 s) SQS moves the message to the DLQ. Backing off to, say, 30 s, 2 min and 8 min means the third attempt lands after the database is back.

options.text: They are lost, because SQS deletes messages that fail three times
options.explanation: Wrong. With a redrive policy, SQS moves messages to the DLQ, it does not delete them. Without one, they would keep retrying until the retention period expired.

options.text: They are dead-lettered; the fix is to set the visibility timeout to 12 hours
options.explanation: Wrong. A 12-hour timeout would survive the outage, but it also means any message whose worker crashes is stuck for 12 hours. Backoff that grows only on failure gives patience without hurting normal failover.

questions.workedExample:
**Current behaviour** (seconds after the first receive; receive count in brackets):

```
0 s    receive (1) fail
30 s   receive (2) fail
60 s   receive (3) fail
90 s   count would be 4 > 3: DLQ
120 s  database back. Too late.
```

1. The retry budget (3 receives, 30 seconds apart) covers only about a minute and a half, shorter than the outage it needs to survive.
2. **With backoff**: on each failure, call `ChangeMessageVisibility` with a delay that grows with the receive count, for example four times longer each time: 30 seconds, then 2 minutes, then 8 minutes.

```
0 s    receive (1) fail, hide 30 s
30 s   receive (2) fail, hide 120 s
150 s  receive (3) succeeds
```

3. The first retry is still quick, but the third attempt now lands after the database is back, so the same receive budget spans the outage.
4. Add jitter (randomise each delay by up to 20% either way) so thousands of messages do not retry in lockstep when the database returns.
5. Note the cap: visibility can be extended to at most 12 hours from the start of the current ReceiveMessage attempt; extending visibility does not reset that attempt's 12-hour limit.

questions.prompt: You are moving a RabbitMQ 3.x cluster that uses classic mirrored queues to **RabbitMQ 4.x**. Assume default quorum delivery-limit settings. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Classic mirrored queues remain a supported option for high availability on 4.x
options.explanation: Wrong. Classic queue mirroring was deprecated for years and removed in RabbitMQ 4.0. Replicated queues on 4.x are quorum queues (or streams), so the migration must happen before or during the upgrade.

options.text: A quorum queue confirms a publish only once a majority of its replicas have written it
options.explanation: Correct. Quorum queues use Raft. A message is committed when a majority of members have it, which is what lets the queue survive a minority of node failures without losing confirmed messages.

options.text: With no dead-letter exchange configured, a message that keeps crashing its consumers is eventually dropped
options.explanation: Correct. Since 4.0, quorum queues have a default delivery limit of 20. A message redelivered more than that is dead-lettered if a dead-letter exchange is configured and otherwise removed, so set up a DLX for anything you cannot afford to lose.

options.text: A 3-replica quorum queue keeps accepting publishes with two of its three nodes down
options.explanation: Wrong. With one of three members left there is no majority, so the queue cannot commit new messages. Three replicas tolerate one failure; tolerating two needs five.

options.text: Quorum queues are always durable and cannot be exclusive, so a temporary per-connection reply queue should stay a classic queue
options.explanation: Correct. Quorum queues are designed for data that must survive failures. Short-lived, exclusive queues, such as RPC reply queues, are a job for classic queues.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Mirroring is gone**: 4.0 removed classic queue mirroring. Quorum queues replace it.
2. **Raft majority**: a quorum queue keeps working only while a majority of its replicas are up, so it can lose just under half of them:

| Replicas | Failures tolerated |
|---|---|
| 3 | 1 |
| 5 | 2 |

With two of three nodes down, one survivor is not a majority, so publishes cannot be confirmed.
3. **Poison messages**: the default `delivery-limit` of 20 means repeated failures counted by that RabbitMQ version eventually remove the message; explicit requeue counting differs across 4.x releases. Without a DLX, removed means gone.
4. **Durability by design**: quorum queues cannot be exclusive or transient, so keep throwaway reply queues classic.

questions.prompt: An SQS FIFO queue uses `MessageGroupId = accountId`. A malformed message for account 77 makes the consumer throw every time it is received. The queue has **no redrive policy**. Assume single-message receives and an order-preserving consumer. What do you observe?

options.text: Account 77's later messages are stuck behind it while other accounts flow normally, until the bad message expires at the end of the retention period
options.explanation: Correct. An in-flight message blocks additional receives for its group until deletion or visibility expiry. On retry the consumer must handle the failed head before later effects. The bad message keeps reappearing after each visibility timeout, blocking account 77 for up to the retention period (4 days by default). Add a redrive policy so it moves to a DLQ after a few attempts.

options.text: The entire queue stops, because FIFO queues deliver strictly one message at a time
options.explanation: Wrong. FIFO ordering is per message group. Messages for other accounts are in other groups and continue to be delivered.

options.text: SQS skips the bad message after the visibility timeout and delivers account 77's next message
options.explanation: Wrong. Skipping would break the per-group ordering guarantee. SQS redelivers the same message until it is deleted or expires.

options.text: SQS moves it to a DLQ automatically after 10 attempts
options.explanation: Wrong. SQS has no default DLQ. Dead-lettering happens only when you configure a redrive policy with a `maxReceiveCount`.

questions.workedExample:
1. FIFO semantics: multiple same-group messages can be returned in one batch. Further receives wait while the batch is in flight; application processing must preserve order and stop at failures.
2. The consumer throws, never deletes, so after each visibility timeout the **same** message reappears.
3. Account 77 is stuck. Other groups are independent, so they flow.
4. Without a redrive policy this continues until the message passes the queue's retention period (default 4 days, up to 14) and is deleted. Lost **and** blocking.
5. Fix: add a DLQ with `maxReceiveCount` of, say, 5. After five failures the message moves aside and account 77's queue unblocks. Alarm on DLQ depth.

Note that skipping the message unblocks the group but means account 77's later messages are processed without it; the consumer should be able to cope, or the key should be parked as described in the ordering lesson.

lessons.title: Independent subscriptions with SNS and SQS
lessons.summary: Give every reacting service its own durable queue and understand partial subscriber completion.
lessons.body:
A queue hands each message to **one** consumer. But many real messages are facts that several systems care about. When an order is placed, billing, shipping, analytics and email all want to know. **Publish/subscribe** (pub/sub) solves this: a publisher sends a message to a **pub/sub topic**, and the broker delivers to each matching subscription according to its delivery guarantees.

## Topics and subscriptions

```
            ┌─▶ sub: billing  ─▶ svc
publisher ─▶│
  (topic)   ├─▶ sub: shipping ─▶ svc
            └─▶ sub: email    ─▶ svc
```

- The **message publisher** knows only the topic name. It has no idea who is listening.
- Each **subscription** is an independent stream of copies with its own delivery state.
- Adding a new consumer means adding a subscription. The publisher does not change or redeploy.

This is the fan-out decoupling from the first lesson: the producer is decoupled from the **number and identity** of consumers.

> [!note] Subscription vs consumer
> In most systems a subscription can itself have several consumers competing for its messages. Google Pub/Sub, Azure Service Bus topics and Kafka consumer groups all work this way: **pub/sub between subscriptions, competing consumers within one**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a newsletter posted to every subscribing household
> A club posts its newsletter to every household on its mailing list. Each household gets its own copy in its own letterbox, and inside a house whoever is free reads it and acts on it. The club never needs to know who lives in each house, and a new family only has to join the list.
>
> **How it maps:** The newsletter is the published message and the mailing list is the topic. Each household's letterbox is a subscription (or an SQS queue in the SNS-to-SQS pattern), and the people inside one house are competing consumers sharing that copy.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real post arrives in no promised order and occasionally twice, which is also true of standard SNS and SQS, but the club cannot see whether one household has acted before another. A broker can also filter which messages each subscription receives, which a printed newsletter cannot.

## The SNS + SQS fan-out pattern

On AWS, SNS is the topic and SQS queues are the subscriptions. This combination is so common that it has a name: **fan-out**.

```
OrderService
     │ publish
     ▼
 [SNS topic: orders]
  │        │        │
  ▼        ▼        ▼
[SQS]    [SQS]    [SQS]
billing  shipping  email
  │        │        │
 workers  workers  workers
```

Why not have each service subscribe to SNS directly over HTTP? Because the queue in between gives each consumer:

- **Durability while it is down.** SNS retries HTTP endpoints for a while, but an SQS queue holds messages for up to 14 days.
- **Its own pace.** Shipping can lag by an hour without affecting billing.
- **Its own retries and DLQ.** A poison message for email does not affect shipping.
- **Independent scaling.** Each queue has its own worker fleet.

Two configuration details trip people up:

1. The SQS queue's **access policy** must allow the SNS topic to send to it.
2. Enable **raw message delivery** if you want the SQS body to be your original payload. Otherwise SNS wraps it in a JSON envelope (`Type`, `MessageId`, `TopicArn`, `Message`...), and your consumer must unwrap it.

SNS FIFO topics can fan out to SQS FIFO queues when ordering within a message group matters.

Delivery to each subscription is independent. Billing may not have created an invoice when Email starts handling the same `OrderPlaced` event. If Email requires an invoice, trigger it from `InvoiceIssued` or use another explicit readiness protocol rather than assuming Billing runs first.

## Key takeaways

- Pub/sub copies a fact to each matching subscription; workers within one queue compete for its copy.
- SNS-to-SQS fan-out isolates each service’s backlog, retry path and worker capacity.
- Configure the queue access policy and either unwrap the SNS envelope or enable raw delivery.
- Independent subscribers do not complete together: publish or check explicit prerequisites.

## Further reading

- [Fanout Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-sqs-as-subscriber.html)
- [Publish–subscribe pattern (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publish%E2%80%93subscribe_pattern)

questions.prompt: An `OrderPlaced` message is published to an SNS topic with three SQS queue subscriptions (billing, shipping, email). Each queue has 4 workers. How many times is the message processed assuming all subscriptions match, delivery succeeds and no duplicates occur?

options.text: Once in total, by whichever of the 12 workers is fastest
options.explanation: Wrong. That is how a single queue behaves. A topic copies the message into every subscription, so each of the three queues gets its own copy.

options.text: 12 times, once per worker
options.explanation: Wrong. Within each SQS queue the 4 workers compete for messages, so only one of them processes each copy. Copies are made per subscription, not per worker.

options.text: 3 times, once per subscription
options.explanation: Correct. SNS delivers one copy to each of the three queues, and in each queue one of the competing workers processes it: pub/sub between subscriptions, competing consumers within one.

options.text: 4 times, once per worker in a single queue
options.explanation: Wrong. This mixes up the two levels. The number of workers per queue changes throughput, not how many copies are processed.

questions.workedExample:
1. SNS fans out one copy to each matching queue subscription under the stated no-duplicates assumption.
2. Workers within each queue compete for its copy; adding workers does not create more subscriptions.
3. Billing, shipping and email therefore each process their own copy once in this scenario.
4. Standard delivery can repeat in real operation, so each subscriber needs duplicate-safe effects.

questions.prompt: A team subscribes their service directly to an SNS topic via HTTPS. During a 3-hour outage of their service, what is the main risk compared with putting an SQS queue between SNS and the service?

options.text: There is no difference; SNS stores messages for 14 days for every subscriber
options.explanation: Wrong. That retention is a property of SQS queues, not SNS topics. Confusing the two is exactly why the fan-out pattern puts a queue in front of each subscriber.

options.text: SNS will deliver messages out of order
options.explanation: Wrong. Standard SNS does not guarantee ordering in either design, so this is not a difference caused by the outage or by adding a queue.

options.text: The publisher will be blocked until the service recovers
options.explanation: Wrong. SNS accepts the publish independently of subscriber health. The publisher is unaffected; the risk is on the subscriber side.

options.text: Messages published during the outage may be lost once SNS exhausts its delivery retries
options.explanation: Correct. SNS retries HTTP/S endpoints according to a delivery policy, but it is not a long-term store. After retries are exhausted the message is dropped (or sent to a subscription DLQ if one is configured). An SQS queue would hold it for up to 14 days.

questions.workedExample:
1. Standard SNS delivery retries are bounded; optional FIFO archive/replay is a separate feature. It pushes each message to each subscription and retries failures for a bounded period.
2. A 3-hour outage exceeds the documented one-hour maximum HTTP/S retry-policy duration, so messages can be dropped.
3. With `SNS → SQS → service`, SNS delivers successfully to SQS (which is up), and SQS holds messages until the service returns.
4. On recovery, the service drains the backlog at its own pace.

This is the main reason the fan-out pattern uses a queue per subscriber.

questions.prompt: Your SQS consumer, subscribed to an SNS topic, fails to parse messages: the body looks like `{"Type":"Notification","MessageId":...,"Message":"{\"orderId\":...}"}`. What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Change the publisher to send plain text instead of JSON
options.explanation: Wrong. The wrapping is added by SNS regardless of payload format. Changing the publisher does not remove the envelope and may break other subscribers.

options.text: Enable raw message delivery on the SNS subscription
options.explanation: Correct. By default SNS wraps the payload in a JSON envelope with metadata. Raw message delivery passes the original payload straight through as the SQS message body.

options.text: Switch the queue to FIFO
options.explanation: Wrong. FIFO affects ordering and deduplication, not the message envelope. The envelope would still be there.

options.text: Add a filter policy so only well-formed messages are delivered
options.explanation: Wrong. Every message is well formed; it is just wrapped. Filter policies decide which messages are delivered, not their format.

questions.workedExample:
1. Recognise the shape: `Type`, `MessageId`, `TopicArn`, `Message` is the SNS **notification envelope**.
2. Your actual payload is the string in `Message`, JSON-encoded a second time (hence the escaped quotes).
3. Two options:
   - Unwrap in code: `JSON.parse(JSON.parse(body).Message)`.
   - Set `RawMessageDelivery=true` on the subscription so the body is the original payload.
4. Raw delivery is cleaner and smaller. Include required metadata in the payload or compatible attributes. Raw SNS-to-SQS delivery allows at most 10 message attributes; messages exceeding that limit are discarded for the raw subscription.

questions.prompt: Billing and Email each consume `OrderPlaced` through their own SQS queue subscribed to one SNS topic. Email's handler calls Billing's API to fetch the invoice PDF. About 2% of confirmation emails fail with "invoice not found", then succeed on retry. What is happening, and what is the best fix?

options.text: SNS sometimes delivers to Email before Billing; use an SNS FIFO topic so Billing is always delivered first
options.explanation: Wrong. FIFO orders messages within a message group; it says nothing about which **subscription** is processed first. Each subscriber's queue and workers run at their own pace.

options.text: The subscribers are independent, so Email sometimes runs before Billing has created the invoice; have Email react to an `InvoiceIssued` event that Billing publishes once the invoice exists
options.explanation: Correct. Fan-out gives each subscriber its own pace, so there is no ordering between them. If Email depends on Billing's result, the dependency should be explicit: Billing publishes a fact when the invoice is ready and Email consumes that.

options.text: Email is processing duplicate deliveries of OrderPlaced
options.explanation: Wrong. A duplicate can race the original and does not prove Billing has finished. Duplicates alone do not explain the missing dependency ordering. The failure is about timing between two subscribers.

options.text: Email's visibility timeout is too short
options.explanation: Wrong. A short visibility timeout causes redelivery during processing, not a missing invoice. The symptom comes from Billing not having finished yet.

questions.workedExample:
1. With fan-out, each subscription is a separate stream with its own backlog, workers and retries.
2. So for any one order, "Billing has processed OrderPlaced" and "Email has processed OrderPlaced" happen in either order.
3. Email assumed Billing was always first: an **implicit** dependency between subscribers. It holds 98% of the time, which makes it dangerous.
4. Make the dependency explicit:

```
OrderPlaced ─▶ Billing
Billing ─▶ InvoiceIssued ─▶ Email
```

5. Alternative: put the data Email needs in the event (event-carried state transfer), if it does not truly depend on Billing's output.

lessons.title: Route events with subscription filters
lessons.summary: Apply SNS filter policies and RabbitMQ topic bindings to deliver only matching events.
lessons.body:
A subscription need not receive every published event. Filtering selects the subset before a worker spends time receiving and discarding it. In the policy below, all three listed fields must match; the array for a field lists its accepted alternatives.

## Filtering

Often a subscriber cares about only some messages. Shipping does not need `OrderCancelled` events for digital goods. Rather than receiving everything and discarding most of it, the subscriber can set a **filter policy**.

```json
{
  "eventType": ["OrderPlaced"],
  "fulfilment": ["physical"],
  "amount": [{ "numeric": [">=", 100] }]
}
```

The example accepts physical `OrderPlaced` messages whose numeric `amount` is at least 100; it does not transform the payload.

SNS evaluates filter policies against **message attributes** by default, or against the message body if you set the filter policy scope to `MessageBody`. Messages that do not match are simply not delivered to that subscription.

Filtering saves consumer compute and queue costs, but it moves routing logic into infrastructure configuration. Keep filter policies in version control alongside the consumer's code.

RabbitMQ achieves similar routing with **topic exchanges**: queues bind with patterns such as `order.*.physical` or `order.#`, where `*` matches one word and `#` matches zero or more.

## Key takeaways

- SNS filters use message attributes by default, with an optional message-body scope.
- RabbitMQ topic bindings use a one-word wildcard and a zero-or-more-word wildcard.
- Keep routing configuration versioned with the subscriber so filtering changes can be reviewed.

## Further reading

- [Amazon SNS message filtering (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-message-filtering.html)
- [AMQP 0-9-1 model explained (RabbitMQ)](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/amqp-concepts)

questions.prompt: Publishers attach `eventType` and `region` as SNS **message attributes**. The EU fulfilment service should receive only `OrderPlaced` events for region `eu`. Which subscription filter policy achieves that?

options.text: `{"eventType": ["OrderPlaced", "eu"]}`
options.explanation: Wrong. Values in one array are OR'd for the same attribute, so this matches eventType OrderPlaced or eventType eu. It does not check region at all.

options.text: `{"region": ["eu"]}`
options.explanation: Wrong. This matches every EU event, including cancellations and refunds, so the service would receive far more than OrderPlaced.

options.text: `{"eventType": ["OrderPlaced"], "region": ["eu"]}`
options.explanation: Correct. Different keys are AND'd, so a message must have eventType OrderPlaced and region eu. This is exactly the requirement.

options.text: `{"eventType": [{"anything-but": ["OrderPlaced"]}], "region": ["eu"]}`
options.explanation: Wrong. anything-but inverts the match, so this delivers every EU event **except** OrderPlaced: the opposite of what is wanted.

questions.workedExample:
SNS filter policy semantics:

1. **Across keys: AND.** Every key in the policy must match.
2. **Within a key's array: OR.** Any listed value matches.
3. Requirement: `eventType` is `OrderPlaced` **and** `region` is `eu`.
4. So: two keys, one value each: `{"eventType":["OrderPlaced"],"region":["eu"]}`.

Since the data is in attributes, the default filter policy scope (`MessageAttributes`) applies. If the fields were in the JSON body, you would set the scope to `MessageBody`.

questions.prompt: A RabbitMQ topic exchange receives a message with routing key `order.uk.physical`. Which of these bindings deliver it to their queue? Select all that apply.

options.text: `order.#`
options.explanation: Correct. `#` matches zero or more words, so it matches `uk.physical` after `order.`.

options.text: `order.*`
options.explanation: Wrong. `*` matches exactly one word. `order.*` matches `order.uk` but not the three-word key `order.uk.physical`.
Correct. Each `*` matches one word: `order` and `physical`, with `uk` matched literally.

options.text: `*.physical`
options.explanation: Wrong. This pattern has two words and the key has three. `*` cannot stretch to cover `order.uk`.

options.text: `#.digital`
options.explanation: Wrong. `#` could absorb `order.uk`, but the last word must be literally `digital`, and the key ends in `physical`.

questions.workedExample:
Split the key into words: `order` · `uk` · `physical` (three words).

| Pattern | Words | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| `order.#` | order + any | ✓ |
| `order.*` | exactly 2 | ✗ |
| `*.uk.*` | exactly 3 | ✓ |
| `*.physical` | exactly 2 | ✗ |
| `#.digital` | ends digital | ✗ |

Rules:
1. `*` = exactly one word.
2. `#` = zero or more words.
3. Everything else must match literally.

A message matching several bindings to **different** queues is copied to each; that is fan-out with filtering.

lessons.title: Push, pull and consumer capacity
lessons.summary: Choose how messages reach a consumer and how overload signals reach the broker.
lessons.body:
The delivery protocol determines who decides when more work arrives. Judge it against processing cost, endpoint reachability and the consumer’s ability to report excess demand.

## Push vs pull consumers

For HTTP push versus polling pull, how does a message reach the consumer? A broker may also push over a connection the consumer originally opened, as RabbitMQ does.

| | Push | Pull |
|---|---|---|
| Who starts | Broker calls you | You ask broker |
| Flow control | Broker guesses | Consumer decides |
| Endpoint | Must be reachable | Can be private |
| Examples | SNS→HTTP, Pub/Sub push | SQS, Kafka |

**Push** delivery (SNS to an HTTPS endpoint, Google Pub/Sub push subscriptions, webhooks) is convenient for serverless handlers: you just expose an endpoint. But the broker controls the rate. If your endpoint slows down, the broker must infer overload from errors or latency and back off. Google Pub/Sub push, for example, uses a slow-start algorithm and reduces its sending rate when it sees failures.

**Pull** delivery (SQS, Kafka, Pub/Sub pull, Kinesis) lets the consumer ask only when it has capacity. This gives natural **backpressure**: a slow consumer simply asks less often, and the backlog builds in the broker, subject to retention, capacity and durability limits. Pull also works for consumers behind firewalls, since they make outbound connections only.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: table service versus a buffet
> At a restaurant with table service, the waiter decides when the next course arrives. If you are still eating, plates pile up unless the waiter notices and slows down. At a buffet you fetch the next plate only when you are ready, and the food simply waits in the serving trays.
>
> **How it maps:** Table service is push: the broker decides the rate and must infer from errors or latency that you are overloaded. The buffet is pull: the consumer asks only when it has capacity, so the backlog waits in the broker. That is natural backpressure.
>
> **Where it stops:** Buffet food goes cold, but a broker keeps messages only within its retention and capacity limits, and a pull consumer pays for every empty trip it makes. A push broker also retries and slows down using explicit signals such as fast error responses, rather than by watching you eat.

RabbitMQ is a hybrid: the broker pushes over a persistent connection, but **consumer prefetch** acts as a credit limit, so the consumer controls how much is in flight.

> [!tip] Rule of thumb
> Prefer **pull** for high-throughput or heavy processing, where flow control matters. Use **push** for low-volume integrations and serverless endpoints, and make sure the endpoint returns errors quickly when overloaded rather than timing out.

## Key takeaways

- HTTP push needs a reachable endpoint; pull consumers initiate outbound fetches when capacity is available.
- Push endpoints must fail promptly on overload so the broker can back off.
- RabbitMQ pushes over a consumer-opened connection, with prefetch controlling in-flight deliveries.

## Further reading

- [Push subscriptions (Google Cloud Pub/Sub)](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/push)
- [AMQP 0-9-1 model explained (RabbitMQ)](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/amqp-concepts)

questions.prompt: Which statements about **pull** consumers compared with HTTP **push** delivery are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pull consumers get natural backpressure, because they request messages only when they have capacity
options.explanation: Correct. A slow pull consumer simply asks less often. The backlog accumulates in the broker, subject to the broker's retention/capacity limits and visible as queue depth or lag.

options.text: Push delivery requires the consumer to expose an endpoint the broker can reach
options.explanation: Correct. For SNS HTTPS or Pub/Sub push, the broker makes inbound requests, so the endpoint must be publicly reachable or otherwise routable from the broker.

options.text: Push always gives lower throughput than pull
options.explanation: Wrong. Push can be very fast and RabbitMQ pushes at high rates. The difference is who controls the rate, not an inherent throughput ceiling.

options.text: Pull consumers can run inside a private network with only outbound connectivity
options.explanation: Correct. Pull consumers initiate connections to the broker, so they work behind firewalls and NAT without opening inbound ports.

options.text: With push, the broker can never adapt its rate to the consumer
options.explanation: Wrong. Push systems do adapt, but indirectly: Google Pub/Sub push uses slow start and backs off on errors, and RabbitMQ limits in-flight messages with prefetch.

questions.workedExample:
Frame it as **who initiates** and **who controls flow**:

| | Push | Pull |
|---|---|---|
| Initiator | Broker | Consumer |
| Network | Inbound to consumer | Outbound only |
| Flow control | Inferred by broker | Explicit, by consumer |

1. Backpressure: pull is explicit, so statement 1 is true.
2. Reachability: push needs an endpoint, so statement 2 is true.
3. Private networks: pull works outbound-only, so statement 4 is true.
4. 'Always lower throughput' and 'never adapts' are absolutes that real systems (RabbitMQ prefetch, Pub/Sub slow start) contradict.

questions.prompt: A Google Pub/Sub **push** subscription delivers to an HTTPS endpoint that writes each message to a database. During a database slowdown the endpoint holds each request for up to 60 seconds before failing, the service runs out of connections, and the outage spreads. What should the endpoint do?

options.text: Return `200` immediately and do the database write in a background thread
options.explanation: Wrong. Acknowledging before the work is done turns delivery into at-most-once: if the process crashes, the message is gone. It also removes the only signal Pub/Sub has that you are overloaded.

options.text: Raise the subscription's acknowledgement deadline to 10 minutes
options.explanation: Wrong. Holding requests even longer ties up more connections and memory. The problem is that the endpoint accepts work it cannot do, not that it is given too little time.

options.text: Fail fast with an error status such as 503 or 429 when it is overloaded, so Pub/Sub slows its push rate and retries later
options.explanation: Correct. Push delivery has no explicit demand signal; the broker infers capacity from responses. Quick errors make Pub/Sub back off, while the unacknowledged messages wait safely in the subscription.

options.text: Disable retries on the subscription so failed messages do not come back
options.explanation: Wrong. That converts a temporary slowdown into data loss. Retries with backoff are what let the backlog drain once the database recovers.

questions.workedExample:
1. With **push**, the broker controls the rate and guesses your capacity from success, failure and latency.
2. A slow failure (60 s) is the worst signal: it consumes resources and tells the broker little.
3. A fast `503`/`429` tells Pub/Sub to reduce its rate quickly; its push flow control backs off on failures.
4. Messages stay unacknowledged in the subscription, durable and visible as backlog.
5. If heavy processing is the norm, consider a **pull** subscription instead: the consumer then asks only when it has capacity, which is explicit backpressure.

lessons.title: Fan-out costs, replay and event buses
lessons.summary: Predict how subscribers multiply traffic and distinguish copied queues from retained logs and routed event buses.
lessons.body:
Adding subscribers changes cost and recovery options. Queue copies isolate processing, while a retained log lets each group remember its own reading position without a separate stored copy.

## Delivery to many: what can go wrong

Fan-out multiplies messages and therefore multiplies costs and failure modes.

- **Cost.** One publish to a topic with 8 SQS subscriptions is 1 SNS publish plus 8 deliveries, then 8 receives and 8 deletes. At 5,000 orders per second that is 80,000 consumer receive/delete SQS API calls per second (fewer with batching).
- **Partial failure.** Delivery to each subscription is independent. Billing may have processed an order that email has not even received yet. Never assume all subscribers are in the same state.
- **Duplicates.** SNS standard topics and SQS standard queues are both at-least-once. Every subscriber must deduplicate independently.
- **Ordering.** Standard SNS gives no ordering guarantee across messages.
- **Slow subscriber.** In a queue-per-subscriber design, one slow consumer's backlog is isolated. In a design where the broker must keep each message until every subscriber has acknowledged it, a slow subscriber can increase storage for everyone.

The cost grows with both the publish rate and the number of subscriptions, because every subscription's consumers must receive, then delete, their own copy of each message. Double the subscriptions and consumer-side traffic doubles; batching up to 10 messages per receive and delete call divides it by the batch size. With full batches of 10, the example above needs about 8,000 calls per second instead of 80,000. Real batches are often only partly full at low traffic, so measure the average batch size before relying on that figure.

## Pub/sub on a log

Kafka implements pub/sub differently. There is no copying: a topic is a set of replicated partition logs, and each consumer group tracks an offset per partition. Adding a new group costs almost nothing extra in storage, and a new group can start from the beginning to process history. The next lesson goes deep on this.

| | SNS + SQS | Kafka |
|---|---|---|
| Copies per sub | One per queue | None (offsets) |
| New sub sees past | Standard fan-out: no; optional SNS FIFO archive/replay differs | Yes, within retention |
| Per-message DLQ | Built in | DIY |

## Event bus services

Managed **event buses** such as Amazon EventBridge add content-based routing rules, schema discovery and many built-in targets on top of pub/sub. They are convenient for integrating many services with moderate volume. For very high throughput or replay-heavy workloads, a log such as Kafka or Kinesis is usually a better fit.

## Key takeaways

- Fan-out multiplies receive/delete traffic by subscriber count; effective batching reduces calls.
- Standard SNS/SQS subscribers must handle duplicates and independent ordering or completion.
- A new standard fan-out subscription gets future deliveries; log consumers can replay retained history.
- Event buses help route integrations, while logs fit high-volume replay-heavy streams.

## Further reading

- [Fanout Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-sqs-as-subscriber.html)
- [Publish–subscribe pattern (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publish%E2%80%93subscribe_pattern)

questions.prompt: A new fraud-analysis team wants to start consuming order events and, on day one, process the **last 7 days of history** before continuing live. Events currently flow through SNS standard topics fanned out to SQS queues. What is the most important constraint they face?

options.text: A new SQS subscription only receives messages published after it was created, so history must come from elsewhere
options.explanation: Correct. SNS does not retain messages for future subscribers (outside the separate SNS FIFO archive and replay feature). In a log such as Kafka, a new consumer group could just start from the earliest retained offset.

options.text: SNS FIFO topics are required before any new subscriber can be added
options.explanation: Wrong. New subscriptions can be added to standard topics at any time. FIFO is about ordering, not about adding subscribers.

options.text: The fraud team must share an existing queue with billing to see past messages
options.explanation: Wrong. Sharing a queue makes the teams competing consumers, so each would see only some of the messages, and messages already processed by billing were deleted.

options.text: SQS cannot hold 7 days of messages
options.explanation: Wrong. SQS retention can be set up to 14 days. The problem is not how long the new queue can hold messages but that messages published before it existed were never delivered to it.

questions.workedExample:
1. In SNS + SQS, copies are made **at publish time**, only into subscriptions that exist then.
2. Each copy is deleted from its queue once that subscriber acknowledges it.
3. So there is no shared history for a newcomer to read.
4. Options for the fraud team:
   - Backfill from the source database or a data lake.
   - Use SNS FIFO's archive and replay, if the topic is FIFO and archiving was enabled beforehand.
   - Longer term, put events on a retained log (Kafka, Kinesis) where a new consumer group can start from `earliest`.

This replayability is one of the strongest reasons teams adopt log-based streaming.

questions.prompt: An SNS topic receives a steady stream of orders and fans out to 6 SQS queues. Each queue's consumers currently receive and delete one message per API call. Six more teams now want their own subscriptions. Assuming no retries or empty polls, which prediction about consumer-side SQS API calls is right?

options.text: Unchanged, because SNS still receives each order only once
options.explanation: Wrong. SNS is published to once, but it delivers a separate copy into every subscribed queue. Each copy must be received and deleted by that queue's consumers, so consumer-side traffic scales with the number of subscriptions.

options.text: It doubles, and batching cannot help because every message still needs its own receive and delete
options.explanation: Wrong on batching. Each message must be received and deleted, but one ReceiveMessage or DeleteMessageBatch call can handle up to 10 messages, so full batches cut the number of calls roughly tenfold.

options.text: It grows about 36-fold, because each new subscription multiplies the existing ones
options.explanation: Wrong. Subscriptions add copies; they do not multiply each other. Twelve subscriptions mean twelve copies of each message, twice as many as six.

options.text: It doubles, because each new subscription receives and deletes its own copy; full batches of 10 could cut the total about tenfold
options.explanation: Correct. Consumer-side calls grow with the publish rate times the number of subscriptions, so going from 6 to 12 doubles them. Batching divides calls by the average batch size, so full batches of 10 bring the doubled total below today's unbatched level.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each subscription needs its own delivered copy, and its workers receive and delete that copy independently.
2. Adding the same number of subscriptions again doubles those consumer operations under the stated assumptions.
3. Batching combines up to ten messages in one receive or batch-delete request, reducing API calls when batches fill.
4. Measure actual batch fill, empty polls and retries before estimating costs; publish and delivery charges are separate.

link.title: Fanout SNS notifications to SQS queues

questions.prompt: An SNS **standard** topic fans out to three SQS standard queues (billing, shipping, email). Which statements about duplicates and ordering are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Because SNS assigns one MessageId per publish, at most one subscriber can ever receive a duplicate
options.explanation: Wrong. Delivery to each subscription is independent and at-least-once, so any or all of the subscribers can receive a copy more than once.

options.text: Each subscriber must deduplicate independently, keyed on a stable event ID
options.explanation: Correct. Each subscriber has its own processing and its own effects, so each needs its own record of what it has already applied.

options.text: A duplicate may reach billing while email receives the message exactly once
options.explanation: Correct. Retries and redeliveries happen per subscription and per queue, so subscribers can see different numbers of copies of the same event.

options.text: An SNS FIFO topic with SQS FIFO queues would give each subscriber ordering within a message group
options.explanation: Correct. SNS FIFO topics can fan out to SQS FIFO queues and preserve order (and deduplication) per message group for each subscription.

options.text: One shared deduplication record keyed only by event ID is sufficient for all three subscribers
options.explanation: Wrong. If billing records the event ID first, shipping and email would see it as already processed and skip their own work. Dedup state must be per subscriber, for example keyed on (subscriber, eventId).

questions.workedExample:
1. Fan-out creates **independent** deliveries. Think of three separate at-least-once channels that share only a source.
2. So duplicates are per channel: billing might see 2 copies, shipping 1, email 1.
3. Therefore dedup is per subscriber. A shared table keyed only by event ID would suppress other subscribers. A shared table keyed by (subscriber, eventId) is valid; commit its record atomically with that subscriber's effects.
4. Ordering: standard SNS and SQS give none. If order within an entity matters, use SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO with `MessageGroupId = entityId`.

questions.prompt: A company has two needs: (a) route about 50 business events per second between 40 internal services and SaaS integrations using content-based rules, and (b) ingest **400,000 clickstream events per second** that data scientists replay from the start whenever a model changes. Which combination fits best?

options.text: An event bus such as EventBridge for both
options.explanation: Wrong. An event bus is designed for integration at moderate volume. EventBridge supports archive/replay and adjustable quotas, so these are not impossible. Its routing model is a less direct fit than independently positioned log readers for this sustained replay-heavy workload; validate quotas and cost.

options.text: SNS + SQS for (b), with a new queue for each replay
options.explanation: Wrong. A new SQS subscription only receives messages published after it was created, so it cannot replay history at all.

options.text: Kafka for (a) and an event bus for (b)
options.explanation: Wrong. This is the wrong way round. Kafka could handle (a), but the event bus is the weak choice for the high-volume, replay-heavy stream.

options.text: An event bus for (a), and a retained log such as Kafka or Kinesis for (b)
options.explanation: Correct. Low-volume integration benefits from managed routing rules and built-in targets. High-throughput clickstream with replay needs a partitioned, retained log where each consumer group can start from the earliest offset.

questions.workedExample:
Match each workload to the tool's strengths:

| Need | Volume | Replay? | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) integration | ~50/s | No | Event bus |
| (b) clickstream | 400k/s | Yes | Log |

1. (a) is about **routing**: many targets, content-based rules, low operational effort.
2. (b) is about **throughput and history**: append-only partitions, retention measured in days, consumers that rewind.
3. Ordinary SNS standard fan-out cannot rewind. SNS FIFO archive/replay is an explicit alternative if enabled in advance; it is not an independent consumer-offset log.
4. Using two tools is normal. Pick per workload, not one tool for everything.

lessons.title: Kafka offsets, partitions and key ordering
lessons.summary: Follow an append-only log and keep one entity’s records in an ordered partition.
lessons.body:
Queues delete messages once they are consumed. Kafka takes a different view: a topic is an **append-only log** that is kept for a configured time, and consumers simply remember **how far they have read**. This one design choice gives Kafka replay, cheap fan-out to many consumers and very high throughput. It also explains most of its sharp edges.

## The log and offsets

A log is an ordered sequence of records. Each record gets a sequential number, its **Kafka offset** (usually just called its offset), when it is appended.

```
partition 0
offset: 0   1   2   3   4   5   6
      [ a | b | c | d | e | f | g ]──▶
              ▲           ▲       append
       group B│    group A│
```

- Producers only ever append to the end.
- Records are immutable. You never update offset 3.
- Each consumer group has its own position. Group A is at 5, group B is at 2. Neither affects the other.

Reading does not remove anything, so adding a tenth consumer group costs network and CPU but no extra storage.

## Partitions: the unit of parallelism

A single log on one disk would cap throughput, so a topic is split into **partitions**, each its own independent log spread across brokers.

```
topic: orders (3 partitions)
 P0 [0][1][2][3][4]      broker 1
 P1 [0][1][2]            broker 2
 P2 [0][1][2][3]         broker 3
```

The producer chooses a partition for every record:

- **With a key**: the producer hashes the key and uses the remainder after dividing by the partition count (the formula below). Equal serialized keys share a partition while partition count and partitioning configuration stay fixed; other clients or custom partitioners can differ.
- **Without a key**: the built-in Java producer stays with one partition until at least `batch.size` bytes have been produced there before it can switch. Keeping records together improves batching.

For keyed records, hashing gives a repeatable placement while the partition count and partitioner stay fixed. The optional reference shows how the default Java client's remainder-based mapping works:

```formula reference
p = h(k) mod N
where
p: the partition the record goes to, numbered from 0 to N − 1
h: the hash function: it turns the key's bytes into a large positive whole number; the default Java client uses murmur2
k: the record's key, for example an account ID
mod: modulo: the remainder after whole-number division; 19 mod 8 = 3 because 19 = 2 × 8 + 3
N: the number of partitions in the topic, here 8
In words: the same key always hashes to the same number, so while the partition count stays the same, every record with that key lands on the same partition.
```

In code, the default Java client writes this as `toPositive(murmur2(serializedKey)) % numPartitions`, where `%` is the modulo operator.

Ordering is guaranteed **only within a partition**. A stable key mapping gives an append order for that key; producer retries and concurrent processing must still preserve the intended business order. There is no ordering between partitions.

> [!warning] Changing partition count breaks key placement
> Adding partitions changes the placement rule, so new records for an existing key may land on a different partition from its older records. The two partitions can be consumed at different speeds, allowing a newer event to overtake an older one. Plan partition counts up front with measured headroom; resizing needs a migration barrier or another explicit ordering protocol.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: readers with separate bookmarks
> Several people read copies of the same book at different speeds, each keeping their own bookmark.
>
> **How it maps:** A partition log is the ordered book, and a consumer group's offset is its bookmark. Moving one bookmark does not move another, and reading a page does not erase it.
>
> **Where it stops:** Kafka can remove old records under retention or compaction. A topic also has several independent partition logs, so there is no single page order across the whole topic.

## Ordering guarantees, precisely

Kafka guarantees that records **in one partition** are stored and delivered in the order the leader appended them. Whether that matches the order your producer *sent* them depends on retries:

- With retries and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection > 1` and **no** idempotence, batch 1 can fail, batch 2 succeed, then batch 1 succeed on retry: reordered.
- With `enable.idempotence=true` (the default since Kafka 3.0), the broker tracks a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers, rejects out-of-order batches and drops duplicates. Ordering is preserved with up to 5 in-flight requests (`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection`, default 5).

Idempotence needs `acks=all`. If you set `acks=1` without explicitly enabling idempotence, the producer quietly turns idempotence off; if you enable it explicitly alongside `acks=1`, the producer refuses to start.

So the full guarantee is: **per partition, per producer, in send order, with idempotence on.**

## Key takeaways

- Offsets identify immutable records inside one partition; reading them does not delete them.
- Stable key mapping places one entity’s records together, while increasing partition count can remap it.
- Producer idempotence preserves retry order within the supported in-flight limit; business order still requires one ordered producer stream and ordered application processing.

## Further reading

- [Apache Kafka documentation: design](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
- [Kafka 4.2 producer configuration](https://kafka.apache.org/42/configuration/producer-configs/)

questions.prompt: A bank publishes account events (`Deposited`, `Withdrew`) to Kafka and needs each account's events processed in producer send order. Assume one ordered producer stream per account, stable partition count, key-respecting partitioning and ordered consumer processing. Which choice preserves that order while allowing different accounts to be processed in parallel?

options.text: Use a single-partition topic so everything is ordered
options.explanation: Wrong. This works for ordering, but it caps the whole system at one consumer and one partition's throughput. You only need ordering per account, not globally.

options.text: Use the account ID as the record key
options.explanation: Correct. The default partitioner hashes the key, so all events for one account land in one partition, which Kafka keeps in order. Different accounts spread across partitions for parallelism.

options.text: Leave the key empty and rely on timestamps to reorder on the consumer
options.explanation: Wrong. Unkeyed records are spread across partitions, and consumers would have to buffer and sort, which never quite works because they cannot know when a late record has stopped arriving.

options.text: Set the topic's retention to infinite
options.explanation: Wrong. Retention controls how long data is kept, not the order it is delivered in.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ordering requirement is per account, so unrelated accounts can proceed independently.
2. Use the account ID as the record key with stable key-respecting partitioning: one account's records share a partition.
3. Different partitions can be assigned to different consumers in the group.
4. Keep producer idempotence and ordered per-account application processing. Changing partition count or key encoding needs a migration plan because it can change placement.

questions.prompt: An `orders` topic keyed by order ID has 8 partitions. To add consumers, an operator increases it to 12 partitions during peak. Shortly afterwards, a consumer processes `OrderShipped` for an order before `OrderPlaced`. Why?

options.text: Adding partitions triggers unclean leader election, which reorders records
options.explanation: Wrong. Adding partitions does not change leadership of existing partitions, and unclean election is about data loss, not reordering.

options.text: Consumers always reprocess from the earliest offset after a rebalance
options.explanation: Wrong. After a rebalance consumers resume from the last committed offset, not the beginning. The ordering problem is about which partition each record went to.

options.text: Idempotent producers stop guaranteeing order when partitions are added
options.explanation: Wrong. Idempotence guarantees in-order, de-duplicated writes per partition. It knows nothing about key placement across partitions.

options.text: The new partitions changed `hash(key) % N`, so later events for in-flight orders went to different partitions from their earlier events
options.explanation: Correct. With 8 partitions an order might map to P3; with 12 it may map to P7. OrderPlaced sits in P3 and OrderShipped in P7, and since there is no ordering across partitions, a different consumer can process P7 first.

questions.workedExample:
1. Changing partition count changes the default keyed placement rule. A later event for an existing order can go to a new partition while its earlier event remains in the old one.
2. The old partition may have a backlog while the new one is nearly empty.
3. Separate consumers can therefore finish OrderShipped before OrderPlaced; Kafka has preserved each partition's order, but no longer provides one lane for that order.
4. Use a controlled migration with an ordering barrier or drain, or a sequence-aware consumer that parks early events. Moving to a new topic alone does not establish that barrier.

lessons.title: Kafka consumer groups, progress and rebalances
lessons.summary: Separate partition ownership from completed work, and choose consumer or share groups for the workload.
lessons.body:
A group’s assignment says who should read a partition; its committed offset says where recovery resumes. Those are distinct from what a worker thread has actually finished.

## Consumer groups

A **consumer group** is a set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Kafka assigns each partition to **exactly one consumer in the group**.

```
6 partitions, group with 3 consumers
 C1 ◀── P0, P1
 C2 ◀── P2, P3
 C3 ◀── P4, P5
```

Consequences:

- **Maximum parallelism equals the number of partitions.** A 7th consumer in a 6-partition group sits idle.
- **Different groups each get every record.** This is how Kafka does pub/sub: billing and analytics are separate groups.
- **Rebalancing.** When a consumer joins, leaves or misses heartbeats (session timeout, 45 s by default for the classic Java consumer; the new consumer protocol uses broker-controlled timeouts), or fails to call `poll()` within `max.poll.interval.ms` (default 5 minutes), partitions are reassigned.

### Rebalance protocols

Rebalancing has been redesigned twice, and which protocol you run makes a big difference during deploys:

| Protocol | During a rebalance |
|---|---|
| Classic, eager | Every consumer stops |
| Classic, cooperative | Only moved partitions pause |
| New (KIP-848) | Broker-driven, incremental |

- **Eager rebalancing** (the original): every consumer revokes all its partitions, then the group reassigns from scratch. A rolling deploy of 30 instances means 30 stop-the-world pauses.
- **Cooperative rebalancing** (`CooperativeStickyAssignor`): consumers keep the partitions they are allowed to keep; only those that move are paused.
- **The new consumer group protocol** (KIP-848) is generally available from **Kafka 4.0**. The broker's group coordinator computes the assignment and hands out changes to each consumer independently, with no group-wide synchronisation barrier. Brokers enable it by default; clients opt in with `group.protocol=consumer`.

**Static membership** (`group.instance.id`) adds one more trick: a consumer that restarts with the same ID within the session timeout can retain its assignment without an otherwise unnecessary rebalance when the rest of the group and subscriptions remain stable.

### Committing offsets

Consumers record progress by **committing offsets** to an internal topic, `__consumer_offsets`. A committed offset of 1,043 means "the next record I want is offset 1,043".

- Commit **after** processing for at-least-once. A crash causes reprocessing from the last commit.
- Commit **before** processing for at-most-once. A crash skips records.
- `enable.auto.commit=true` uses a default 5-second auto-commit interval; scheduling details depend on client/protocol, which can commit offsets of records you have not finished processing if you hand work to other threads.

Because a consumer commits a single position per partition, a consumer group has no per-message ack. A strictly sequential handler can be blocked by one slow record. Parallel processing is possible, but contiguous offset commits and required per-key order still need coordination. This is the fundamental difference from a queue, and the ordering lesson covers how to deal with it.

> [!note] Share groups: queues on Kafka
> Kafka 4.0 shipped an early version of **share groups** (KIP-932, "queues for Kafka"), and Kafka 4.2 (2026) made them production-ready. Consumers in a share group cooperatively read the same partitions, each record is locked to one consumer and **acknowledged individually**, and delivery attempts are counted. You can then run more consumers than partitions, at the cost of per-partition ordering. Use them for job-style work; keep consumer groups for ordered streams.

## Key takeaways

- A conventional consumer group assigns each partition to one consumer, so extra consumers can sit idle.
- Commit the next offset after completed processing; polling into a worker pool does not mean that work is done.
- Incremental rebalance protocols and stable membership reduce unnecessary assignment pauses.
- Kafka 4.2 share groups provide per-record acquisition and acknowledgement for independent jobs.

## Further reading

- [Kafka consumer design (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/kafka/design/consumer-design.html)
- [KIP-848: the next generation of the consumer rebalance protocol](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-848%3A+The+Next+Generation+of+the+Consumer+Rebalance+Protocol)
- [KIP-932: Queues for Kafka (share groups)](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-932%3A+Queues+for+Kafka)
- [Kafka 4.2 consumer configuration](https://kafka.apache.org/42/configuration/consumer-configs/)

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions. You scale the `billing` consumer group to 8 instances to handle a backlog. What happens?

options.text: Throughput rises by about a third, because work is spread over 8 consumers instead of 6
options.explanation: Wrong. Kafka assigns each partition to only one consumer in a group, so at most 6 consumers can be active. The extra two receive no partitions.

options.text: Two partitions are shared by two consumers each, so some records are processed twice
options.explanation: Wrong. Partitions are never shared within one group. Duplicates in Kafka come from reprocessing after a crash or rebalance, not from shared ownership.

options.text: Kafka automatically splits partitions so each consumer gets one
options.explanation: Wrong. Kafka never changes a topic's partition count automatically. An operator must add partitions, and doing so remaps keys.

options.text: 6 consumers each own one partition and 2 sit idle
options.explanation: Correct. Within a group, a partition has exactly one owner. Parallelism is capped at the partition count; idle consumers act only as hot standbys for a rebalance.

questions.workedExample:
1. A conventional consumer group assigns a partition to one member at a time.
2. The six partitions can keep six members assigned, leaving two without partitions.
3. More group members alone cannot divide an existing partition. Internal processing concurrency is possible, but needs completion tracking and any required per-key ordering.
4. Adding partitions affects keyed placement, so plan that change with ordering and migration requirements in mind.

questions.prompt: A consumer uses `enable.auto.commit=true`. Its poll loop hands each record to a thread pool and immediately polls again. After a crash, the team discovers some records were **never processed**. What happened?

options.text: Auto-commit committed offsets for records that had been polled but were still queued in the thread pool, so the restart resumed past them
options.explanation: Correct. Auto-commit can commit offsets for records that were polled but remain unfinished in the worker pool. The default interval is 5 seconds; scheduling differs between the classic and new consumer protocols. Polling does not mean processed, so a crash can leave recovery past unfinished work.

options.text: Kafka deleted the records because retention expired during the crash
options.explanation: Wrong. Retention can remove older records even during a short outage, but it does not explain the demonstrated commit-ahead race. And expired records would affect every group, not just skip a few in the middle.

options.text: A rebalance assigned those partitions to two consumers, each of which skipped half
options.explanation: Wrong. A partition has one owner per group. Rebalances cause duplicates (reprocessing from the last commit), not skipped records.

options.text: The broker's high watermark moved backwards
options.explanation: Wrong. The high watermark only advances for committed data. Consumers never see records beyond it, and it would not cause skipping of records already read.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline for partition 0:

```
poll() → offsets 100–599
hand to pool; pool done up to 250
poll() → auto-commit 600
crash
restart: resume at 600
251–599 never processed
```

1. Kafka's committed offset is a promise: "everything before this is done".
2. Auto-commit makes that promise based on what was **polled**, not what was **processed**.
3. With synchronous processing inside the poll loop, auto-commit is effectively at-least-once. With asynchronous hand-off it can lose unprocessed work as well as duplicate processed work; it is not a clean end-to-end at-most-once guarantee.
4. Fix: disable auto-commit and commit the next offset after the highest contiguous processed record per partition (track completions, commit with `commitSync`/`commitAsync`).

questions.prompt: A consumer group of 30 instances uses the classic protocol with the eager `RangeAssignor`. Every rolling deploy causes several minutes during which the **whole group** processes nothing, and lag spikes on every partition. Which change helps most directly?

options.text: Move to incremental rebalancing (the KIP-848 protocol with `group.protocol=consumer` on Kafka 4.0+, or the `CooperativeStickyAssignor`) and add static membership with `group.instance.id`
options.explanation: Correct. Eager rebalancing revokes all assignments during membership changes. Incremental protocols let unaffected assignments continue, and static membership can avoid an unnecessary rebalance when an instance returns within the session timeout with stable membership and subscriptions.

options.text: Add partitions so each rebalance has less work per consumer
options.explanation: Wrong. The pause comes from every consumer stopping during each rebalance, not from the amount of work per partition. More partitions can make rebalances slower, and they remap keys.

options.text: Raise `max.poll.interval.ms` to 30 minutes
options.explanation: Wrong. That setting controls how long a consumer may go between polls before it is considered stuck. It does not change the stop-the-world behaviour of eager rebalancing, and a large value delays detection of genuinely stuck consumers.

options.text: Enable auto-commit so offsets are saved during rebalances
options.explanation: Wrong. Commit strategy affects how much work is repeated after a rebalance, not how long the group stops for. Auto-commit can also skip records with asynchronous processing.

questions.workedExample:
1. A rolling deploy repeatedly changes membership. With eager assignment, those changes can pause the whole group.
2. Cooperative assignment or the newer broker-driven protocol keeps unaffected assignments running while changed assignments are transferred.
3. Static membership can preserve an assignment across a short restart when identity, group membership and subscriptions remain suitable; it is not an unconditional guarantee.
4. On Kafka 4.0+, clients opt into the new protocol with group.protocol=consumer. Validate protocol migration and client compatibility before rollout.
