questions.prompt: A 6-partition topic carries **independent** thumbnail jobs that take 2–30 seconds each. You want 60 workers, per-job retries and delivery counts, and you do not care about order. You run Kafka 4.2. What is the best fit?

options.text: A consumer group with 60 instances
options.explanation: Wrong. A consumer group assigns each partition to one consumer, so 54 of the 60 instances would sit idle. And one 30-second job would still block everything behind it in its partition.

options.text: Give each worker its own consumer group
options.explanation: Wrong. Every group receives every record, so all 60 workers would generate every thumbnail. That is pub/sub, not work sharing.

options.text: Increase the topic to 60 partitions and keep a consumer group
options.explanation: Wrong. This makes 60 consumers possible, but each slow job still blocks its partition, retries remain do-it-yourself, and you have created many partitions just to work around the consumption model.

options.text: A share group, in which consumers acquire and acknowledge individual records and can outnumber the partitions
options.explanation: Correct. Share groups (KIP-932, production-ready in Kafka 4.2) give queue semantics on a Kafka topic: records are locked to one consumer at a time, acknowledged or released individually, and delivery attempts are counted. Ordering is given up, which this workload does not need.

questions.workedExample:
1. List the requirements: more workers than partitions, per-record ack and retry, no ordering.
2. **Consumer groups** are built for ordered streams: one owner per partition and one committed offset per partition. Those defaults do not provide per-record broker acknowledgement or let 60 group members own 6 partitions. An application worker pool can add concurrency, but must coordinate retries and commits itself.
3. **Share groups** are built for job queues:
   - many consumers per partition
   - each record acquired with a time-limited lock
   - acknowledge, release or reject per record
   - delivery count per record, so poison records can be capped
4. Before Kafka 4.x the usual answers were more partitions plus an in-consumer worker pool, or a separate queue such as SQS or RabbitMQ.

lessons.title: Kafka replication, ISR and durable acknowledgements
lessons.summary: Combine replication factor, the in-sync minimum and producer acknowledgements without trusting unsafe defaults.
lessons.body:
A successful publish is only as durable as the acknowledgement rule behind it. Read the producer setting together with the topic’s in-sync replica minimum and the cluster’s failure state.

## Replication and the ISR

Each partition has a **replication factor** (typically 3). One replica is the **leader**; all reads and writes go through it by default. **Followers** fetch from the leader to stay up to date.

```
P0: leader b1, followers b2, b3
producer ─▶ b1 ──fetch── b2
             └──fetch── b3
```

The **in-sync replica set (ISR)** is the leader plus the followers that have caught up within `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (default 30 s). The **high watermark** marks the replication-committed boundary. Advancing it requires the record on every current ISR member; modern Kafka's strict minimum-ISR rule also requires the ISR size to meet `min.insync.replicas`. Consumers cannot read beyond this boundary, and transactional `read_committed` consumers can stop earlier at an unresolved transaction.

Durability comes from combining three settings:

| Setting | Typical safe value |
|---|---|
| `replication.factor` | 3 |
| `min.insync.replicas` | 2 |
| producer `acks` | `all` |

With `acks=all`, the leader acknowledges only when all **current** ISR members have the record. `min.insync.replicas` sets a floor on how many replicas that must be; it does not make the leader wait for replicas already outside the ISR.

With three replicas and `min.insync.replicas=2`, one follower can drop out and writes can continue. If both drop out, only the leader remains and writes are refused with a not-enough-replicas error. Successful acknowledgement therefore requires at least two in-sync copies. With all three initially healthy and controller quorum available, one replica failure need not lose acknowledged data; detection and leader election can still cause pauses or transient write errors.

Since **Kafka 3.0** the producer defaults favour durability: `acks=all` and `enable.idempotence=true`. But the broker default for `min.insync.replicas` is still **1**. If both followers fall behind and drop out of the ISR, the ISR is just the leader, and `acks=all` is satisfied by the leader alone. A write acknowledged in that state is guaranteed on only one broker; follower copies may or may not exist, and Kafka replication acknowledgement is not a per-write fsync guarantee. Set `min.insync.replicas=2` explicitly on topics that matter.

With `acks=1` (the default before 3.0), the leader acknowledges as soon as it has written locally. If it dies before followers fetch, the acknowledged write is lost when a follower becomes leader. With `acks=0` the producer does not wait at all.

> [!note] Unclean leader election
> If no ISR replica is available, eligible-leader-replica (ELR) tracking in newer Kafka can identify other safe candidates. Without a safe candidate, Kafka must wait or permit unclean election that risks data loss. `unclean.leader.election.enable` defaults to `false`: Kafka chooses consistency.

Cluster metadata, including which broker leads each partition and the ISR of every partition, is managed by the **KRaft** controller quorum: a small set of controller nodes (typically 3 or 5) that replicate a metadata log among themselves using a Raft-style protocol. One controller is active; brokers follow the metadata log and apply changes. KRaft became production-ready in Kafka 3.3, and **ZooKeeper support was removed entirely in Kafka 4.0** (2025), so clusters must migrate to KRaft on 3.x before upgrading. Like any majority quorum, 3 controllers tolerate one failure and 5 tolerate two.

## Key takeaways

- acks=all waits for the current ISR, whose size can shrink; it does not mean every configured replica.
- An explicit minimum of two in-sync replicas prevents acknowledged writes on the leader alone.
- A surviving leader can serve previously committed records while insufficient ISR size blocks writes.
- Kafka 4.x metadata lives in KRaft; leader-election safety and controller quorum availability remain part of recovery.

## Further reading

- [Apache Kafka documentation: design](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
- [Kafka replication design (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/kafka/design/replication.html)
- [Apache Kafka 4.2: eligible leader replicas and strict minimum ISR](https://kafka.apache.org/42/operations/eligible-leader-replicas/)

questions.prompt: A producer uses `acks=1`. It sends a record; the leader writes it to its log and acknowledges. Before any follower fetches the record, the leader's machine dies and a follower becomes leader. What happens to the record?

options.text: The producer automatically resends it, because the follower never acknowledged
options.explanation: Wrong. The producer already got a success response, so it has no reason to retry. That is exactly what makes acks=1 dangerous.

options.text: It is safe, because the old leader will replay it when it restarts
options.explanation: Wrong. When the old broker rejoins as a follower, it truncates its log back to the new leader's state. The record is discarded, not replayed.

options.text: It is lost, even though the producer was told it succeeded
options.explanation: Correct. With acks=1 only the leader had the record. The new leader never received it, and when the old leader returns it truncates its log to match, so the acknowledged write disappears.

options.text: Kafka blocks the leader election until a replica with the record returns
options.explanation: Wrong. The follower was in the ISR, so its election is a normal clean election. The record was never committed (never reached the high watermark), so Kafka does not wait for it.

questions.workedExample:
```
1. P → leader b1: write r (offset 100)
2. b1 → P: ack   (acks=1)
3. b1 crashes; b2 has up to 99
4. b2 elected leader (clean)
5. b1 returns, truncates to 99
```

1. The record was **acknowledged** but never **committed** (not on all ISR replicas).
2. Committed data survives leader failover; uncommitted data may not.
3. Fix: `acks=all` with `min.insync.replicas=2`, so the ack implies at least two copies.
4. Cost: produce latency rises by roughly one replication round trip, with latency depending on replication lag, batching, load and network conditions.

questions.prompt: A topic has `replication.factor=3` and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Producers use `acks=all`. All three replicas were in sync; both followers fail while the leader and controller quorum remain available. What do producers and consumers of that partition experience?

options.text: Producers get NotEnoughReplicas errors; consumers can still read committed records from the surviving leader
options.explanation: Correct. min.insync.replicas enforces durability on writes: with ISR size 1 < 2, acks=all writes are refused. Reads are unaffected, so consumers keep reading data that was already committed.

options.text: Both producers and consumers carry on normally using the surviving replica
options.explanation: Wrong. The surviving leader would be the only ISR member, which is below min.insync.replicas=2, so it rejects acks=all writes.

options.text: Kafka elects an out-of-sync replica so writes can continue
options.explanation: Wrong. That is unclean leader election, which is disabled by default. In any case one replica survives and is already in the ISR, so no unclean election is needed; the issue is ISR size, not leadership.

options.text: Producers succeed but their writes are silently stored on only one broker
options.explanation: Wrong. That would happen with acks=1. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, Kafka refuses rather than silently weakening durability.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both followers fail and eventually leave the ISR; only the leader remains.
2. The topic requires two in-sync replicas for acks=all writes. The surviving leader cannot meet that minimum, so producers see failures rather than a successful single-copy acknowledgement.
3. The live leader can still serve already committed data to consumers.
4. This trades write availability for the configured durability floor. It does not protect against losing the final surviving copy.

questions.prompt: A topic has `replication.factor=3`, and nobody changed `min.insync.replicas` from the broker default. Producers use a recent client with default settings. During a network problem both followers stop fetching and fall out of the ISR for several minutes, and the leader keeps acknowledging writes. Then the leader's disk fails. What happens to the writes acknowledged during those minutes?

options.text: They are safe: the default `acks=all` means all three replicas had them
options.explanation: Wrong. `acks=all` waits for every replica **currently in the ISR**, not every replica that exists. With both followers out, the ISR was just the leader.

options.text: They never happened: the leader rejected them with NotEnoughReplicas
options.explanation: Wrong. That needs `min.insync.replicas=2`. The broker default is 1, and an ISR of one leader satisfies it, so the writes were accepted.

options.text: They can be lost: with `min.insync.replicas=1`, the leader alone satisfied `acks=all`, so those writes existed only on the failed disk
options.explanation: Correct. This is the trap in Kafka's defaults: the producer is safe by default since 3.0, but the broker's min ISR is not. Setting `min.insync.replicas=2` would have refused the writes instead, so producers would have retried rather than lost data.

options.text: They are lost only if unclean leader election is enabled
options.explanation: Wrong. Unclean election only decides what happens next: promote an out-of-sync follower (available, missing those writes) or stay offline until the old leader returns (which it cannot, its disk is gone). Either way, the writes existed nowhere else.

questions.workedExample:
1. The producer waits for every current ISR member, but the topic still permits an ISR containing only the leader.
2. The followers stopped fetching, so records written during this interval have no follower copy.
3. The leader acknowledges them and then loses its disk. Those records are gone regardless of which leader is chosen next.
4. Set an appropriate min.insync.replicas value with acks=all and retry failures within a deliberate policy; a producer acknowledgement is only as strong as the full replication configuration.

questions.prompt: A Kafka 4.x deployment uses KRaft, replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=1, and a producer with acks=all and enable.idempotence=true. Which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: A successful acknowledgement always proves three replicas have the record
options.explanation: Wrong. acks=all waits for current ISR members, and the configured minimum permits an ISR of one.

options.text: Supported retries within a producer session can avoid duplicate log appends
options.explanation: Correct. Producer idempotence uses identity and sequence information to recognise retry duplicates; it does not deduplicate arbitrary business events.

options.text: The leader waits for the current ISR before acknowledging an acks=all write
options.explanation: Correct. The guarantee is about current in-sync replicas, not every configured replica.

options.text: External API calls made by consumers are automatically exactly once
options.explanation: Wrong. Producer idempotence does not make consumer effects in another system atomic.

options.text: Partition leadership must also be stored in ZooKeeper
options.explanation: Wrong. Kafka 4.x uses KRaft metadata; ZooKeeper support was removed in 4.0.

questions.workedExample:
1. Read the producer and topic settings together: all current ISR members must acknowledge, but the topic permits that set to shrink to the leader alone.
2. Producer idempotence addresses retry appends within its scope; it does not make every later business effect duplicate-safe.
3. KRaft is the metadata coordination system in this deployment.
4. Evaluate durability, duplicate handling and metadata availability separately rather than treating one setting as an end-to-end guarantee.

lessons.title: Kafka retention, compaction and partition capacity
lessons.summary: Choose what history survives and size consumer parallelism from measured throughput.
lessons.body:
Kafka’s retained storage is also a recovery resource. Decide whether consumers need a full event history or the latest value for each key, then check that enough partition and storage capacity supports the workload.

## Retention and compaction

Each partition is stored as a series of **segment files** (1 GiB by default). Old data is removed a whole segment at a time according to the topic's `cleanup.policy`.

| Policy | Keeps |
|---|---|
| `delete` | Whole eligible segments removed when configured age or size limits are exceeded; deletion is asynchronous |
| `compact` | At least the latest record for each key |
| `compact,delete` | Latest per key, but also age-limited |

**Log compaction** turns a topic into a durable table of "latest value per key". In the sketch below, k1, k2 and k3 are record keys, a to d are their values, and `k2=null` is a record for k2 with no value:

```
before: k1=a k2=b k1=c k3=d k2=null
after:  k1=c k3=d   (k2 tombstoned)
```

A record with a `null` value is a **tombstone**: it tells compaction to remove the key entirely (after `delete.retention.ms`, default 24 hours, so consumers have a bounded opportunity to see deletion). A rebuilding consumer must catch up within the tombstone-retention window; otherwise it can miss a delete and retain stale state. Compacted topics back Kafka Streams state stores, `__consumer_offsets` itself, and change-data-capture topics that need to be replayable from scratch.

Compaction never touches the **active segment**, and it keeps record offsets unchanged, so offsets in a compacted topic have gaps.

## Why Kafka is fast

- **Sequential I/O.** Appends and reads are sequential, which disks and SSDs handle at hundreds of MB/s.
- **Page cache.** Kafka leans on the operating system's cache rather than its own; consumers near the head of the log read from memory.
- **Zero-copy.** Brokers use `sendfile` to move bytes from page cache to socket without copying through user space (when TLS is not in use).
- **Batching and compression.** Producers batch records per partition (`linger.ms`, `batch.size`) and compress whole batches with lz4 or zstd.

Benchmark payload sizes, replication, compression and consumer work for the intended deployment; there is no universal cluster throughput figure.

## Choosing the number of partitions

Partitions bound consumer parallelism, so size for the slowest consumer. Measure one consumer's processing rate, then divide the target throughput by it:

```formula reference
P ≥ T / c
where
P: the number of partitions
≥: is at least
T: the target throughput of the topic, here 60 megabytes per second (MB/s)
c: the measured processing rate of one consumer, here 5 MB/s
MB: megabytes
s: seconds; "MB/s" means megabytes per second
In words: enough partitions must be available to assign work to the consumers needed at the measured rate; this estimate assumes balanced traffic and sufficient broker and downstream capacity.
```

In the illustrative workload, twelve equally busy consumers would just keep up. Add measured headroom for growth and failures, because adding partitions later remaps keys. Extra partitions alone do not add workers or make an overloaded database faster.

Too many partitions cost broker memory, open files, longer leader elections and slower rebalances. Reliable limits depend on Kafka version, controller/broker resources and workload; test failover and rebalance behaviour at the planned scale.

## Key takeaways

- Retention removes eligible segments asynchronously; compaction preserves current key state and stable offsets.
- Consumers rebuilding a compacted table must observe deletions before tombstones expire.
- Batching, compression, page cache and sequential I/O explain the design; benchmark deployment throughput.
- Size partition parallelism for the slowest consumer with growth headroom, then validate broker and controller costs.

## Further reading

- [Apache Kafka documentation: design](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
- [Kafka log compaction (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/kafka/design/log_compaction.html)
- [Kafka consumer design (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/kafka/design/consumer-design.html)
- [Apache Kafka (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Kafka)

questions.prompt: A `customer-profiles` topic uses `cleanup.policy=compact` and is keyed by customer ID. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: After compaction, the latest non-deleted value for each customer ID is retained
options.explanation: Correct. That is compaction's guarantee: a consumer rebuilding from the earliest available offset can recover current key state, provided it catches up before relevant tombstones are removed.

options.text: Compaction renumbers offsets so the log has no gaps
options.explanation: Wrong. Offsets are permanent identifiers; compaction removes records but keeps the remaining ones' offsets, so a compacted log has gaps.

options.text: Producing a record with a null value for a customer eventually removes that customer from the topic
options.explanation: Correct. A null-value record is a tombstone. Compaction removes earlier values for the key and, after delete.retention.ms, the tombstone itself.

options.text: Records in the active (currently written) segment can be compacted immediately
options.explanation: Wrong. The active segment is never compacted. Only closed segments are cleaned, so recent duplicates of a key coexist until the segment rolls.

options.text: A new consumer can rebuild current profiles from the earliest available offset if it catches up within the tombstone-retention window
options.explanation: Correct. This is the main use of compacted topics: a durable, replayable 'latest value per key' snapshot, which is how Kafka Streams restores state stores.

questions.workedExample:
Picture the log before and after compaction. Each entry is written offset:key=value, so `2:k1=c` is the record at offset 2 with key k1 and value c:

```
before: 0:k1=a 1:k2=b 2:k1=c 3:k2=null
after:  2:k1=c 3:k2=null
later:  2:k1=c   (tombstone removed)
```

1. k1 keeps only its latest value `c` → statement 1 true.
2. Offsets 2 and 3 keep their numbers → statement 2 false.
3. k2's tombstone removes it, then itself → statement 3 true.
4. The active segment is left alone → statement 4 false.
5. Reading from the earliest available offset within the required retention window recovers every live key → statement 5 true.

questions.prompt: Load tests show that the planned consumers would only just keep up with peak traffic on a new keyed Kafka topic. The team wants growth and failure headroom. Keys are balanced today. Which planning approach is best?

options.text: Choose exactly enough partitions for today's minimum worker count
options.explanation: Wrong. A group cannot assign partitions to more consumers than it has partitions, leaving no room for worker growth.

options.text: Allow measured partition and worker headroom, then validate broker and database capacity
options.explanation: Correct. More parallel assignments can help only when enough workers and downstream capacity exist. Headroom must be tested, including recovery.

options.text: Set the partition count equal to the broker count
options.explanation: Wrong. Consumer processing capacity and key distribution also matter; a broker can host many partitions.

options.text: Choose an arbitrarily huge partition count
options.explanation: Wrong. Partitions consume resources and affect failover and rebalances. Unmeasured excess has a cost.

questions.workedExample:
1. Measure consumer processing with realistic payloads and downstream calls.
2. Plan enough partitions to support the worker fleet needed for peak traffic plus justified headroom.
3. Check key skew, replication costs, broker resources and shared database limits; adding partitions cannot cure a hot key or an overloaded database.
4. Test failover and rebalances. Growing a keyed topic later can remap records, so capacity planning also protects ordering.

lessons.title: Delivery semantics at a failure boundary
lessons.summary: Distinguish possible loss, duplicate delivery and exactly-once effects under explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
Every messaging system has to answer one question: if something fails mid-flight, **might a message be lost, duplicated, or neither?** The answer is the system's **delivery semantics**. Getting this right is the difference between a payment taken once and a payment taken twice.

## Why this is hard

Consider a consumer that processes a message and then acknowledges it. There are two failure points:

```
receive ─▶ process ─▶ ack
         ✗1         ✗2
```

- Crash at ✗1 (before processing completes): if the broker already considered the message done, it is **lost**.
- Crash at ✗2 (after processing, before the ack reaches the broker): the broker redelivers, so it is **duplicated**.

The broker cannot tell these apart. It only knows it did not get an ack. Neither can the producer when a publish times out: did the broker store it or not? This is a form of the [Two Generals' Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Generals%27_Problem): over an unreliable network, no finite exchange of messages lets both sides be certain the other knows.

## The three semantics

| Semantics | Loss? | Duplicates? | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| At-most-once | Possible | No | Ack before work |
| At-least-once | No | Possible | Ack after work, retry |
| Exactly-once | No | No | At-least-once + dedup |

These categories describe a defined failure model and processing boundary. Early acknowledgement does not remove duplicates already introduced by producers or an at-least-once broker; retention expiry and permanent failures can defeat eventual processing. Exactly-once effects require atomic effect/dedup state and sufficient retry/dedup retention.

**At-most-once** suits data where loss is tolerable and duplicates are harmful or pointless: metrics sampling, some telemetry, "typing…" indicators.

**At-least-once** is the default for almost everything: SQS, SNS, RabbitMQ with manual acks, Kafka with commit-after-processing.

**Exactly-once** *delivery* across a network is impossible in general. What systems actually provide is **exactly-once processing** (often called *effectively-once*): messages may be delivered more than once, but their **effects** are applied once.

> [!note] Name the guarantee's boundary
> Retrying delivery while making repeated effects harmless is a common way to achieve effectively-once processing. Check how effects and progress commit together, how long duplicates can be recognised, and which failures the guarantee covers.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a lost receipt
> You pay at a shop, but the receipt printer fails. The missing receipt alone cannot tell you whether the payment went through.
>
> **How it maps:** The receipt is the acknowledgement. Its absence does not distinguish an unsuccessful effect from a successful effect whose acknowledgement was lost. A stable operation ID lets the system recognise a retry.
>
> **Where it stops:** Human staff can investigate directly. An automated consumer needs durable duplicate handling coordinated with the effect; simply remembering that an attempt started is insufficient.

## Key takeaways

- A missing acknowledgement does not reveal whether the consumer finished its effect.
- Acknowledging before work trades retry duplicates for possible loss under the stated boundary.
- Exactly-once effects require safe duplicate handling, atomic state changes and a sufficient retention horizon.

## Further reading

- [Kafka message delivery semantics (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/kafka/design/delivery-semantics.html)
- [Idempotent Receiver (Enterprise Integration Patterns)](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/IdempotentReceiver.html)

questions.prompt: Assume a broker that never redelivers after successful acknowledgement, no duplicate publishes, and no lost acknowledgements. A consumer **acknowledges a message as soon as it receives it**, then processes it. Which delivery semantics does this give?

options.text: At-most-once
options.explanation: Correct. If the consumer crashes after the ack but before finishing, the broker will not redeliver, so the message is lost. It will never be processed twice, so it is at most once.

options.text: At-least-once
options.explanation: Wrong. At-least-once needs the ack to happen after processing, so a crash causes redelivery. Here the broker has already forgotten the message before work begins.

options.text: Exactly-once
options.explanation: Wrong. Exactly-once processing would require both no loss and no duplicates. Early acking removes duplicates only by accepting loss.

options.text: It depends on the broker's replication factor
options.explanation: Wrong. Replication protects messages stored on the broker. Once the consumer has acked, the broker discards the message however many replicas it had, so replication cannot save it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Order of operations: **ack → process**.
2. Crash between them: broker thinks done, work not done → **lost**.
3. Can it be processed twice? Only if redelivered, and the broker has no reason to redeliver after an ack → **no duplicates**.
4. Loss possible, duplicates impossible → **at-most-once**.

Swap the order (process → ack) and the analysis flips to at-least-once.

questions.prompt: Why is true exactly-once **delivery** between a broker and a consumer over a network considered impossible in general?

options.text: Because networks reorder packets
options.explanation: Wrong. TCP already restores packet order within a connection. Reordering is not the obstacle; uncertainty about whether the other side completed is.

options.text: Because it would require global clocks
options.explanation: Wrong. The impossibility does not depend on clocks. Even with perfect clocks, a lost ack is indistinguishable from lost processing.

options.text: Because brokers do not replicate messages
options.explanation: Wrong. Most production brokers replicate. Replication protects against broker failure but does nothing about the ambiguity of an unacknowledged delivery.

options.text: Because after a timeout the sender cannot know whether the receiver processed the message, so it must either risk loss or risk a duplicate
options.explanation: Correct. A missing ack could mean the message never arrived or that only the ack was lost. No finite protocol removes that uncertainty (the Two Generals' Problem), so systems get exactly-once effects through deduplication instead.

questions.workedExample:
1. Broker sends message m. It waits for an ack.
2. No ack arrives. Possible worlds:
   - (a) m never arrived → must resend.
   - (b) m processed, ack lost → must not resend.
3. The broker cannot distinguish (a) from (b).
4. Resend → duplicates in world (b). Don't resend → loss in world (a).
5. Way out: resend always (at-least-once), and have the receiver recognise m's ID and ignore it the second time. Delivery is still 'at least once'; **effects** are once.

lessons.title: Make database consumer effects idempotent
lessons.summary: Use absolute state, atomic deduplication and versions to tolerate retries and replay.
lessons.body:
Delivery can repeat even when the application must apply an effect once. Keep the evidence that an effect happened beside the effect itself, so neither can commit alone.

## Idempotent consumers

An operation is **idempotent** if applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once. Design consumers so a redelivered message does no harm.

### 1. Naturally idempotent operations

Some operations are idempotent by construction:

| Not idempotent | Idempotent |
|---|---|
| `balance += 10` | `SET status='SHIPPED'` |
| `INSERT` new row | `UPSERT` by natural key |
| Send email | Provider-enforced dedup key |

Prefer **absolute state** ("order 17 is shipped") over **deltas** ("add one to shipped count") in message design where you can.



### 2. Deduplication by message ID

When the operation is not naturally idempotent, record which messages you have processed, **in the same transaction as the effect**:

This SQL fragment assumes `processed_messages.id` is a primary key and account 42 exists. The application must roll back a failed transaction before acknowledging a duplicate.

```sql
BEGIN;
-- Claim the ID beside its database effect.
INSERT INTO processed_messages(id)
  VALUES ('msg-8f3a'); -- PK: fails if seen
-- This addition is safe only with the
-- claim.
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10
  WHERE id = 42;
-- Commit both the claim and effect
-- together.
COMMIT;
```

If the message is redelivered, the insert violates the primary key, the transaction rolls back, and the consumer acks the duplicate. Because the dedup record and the effect commit atomically, there is no window where one exists without the other.

> [!warning] Dedup outside the transaction is racy
> "Check Redis for the ID, do the work, then write the ID to Redis" fails two ways: a crash after the work but before the Redis write causes a duplicate, and concurrent consumers can both see "not processed". An atomic Redis claim alone does not close the gap to a separate database effect: a crash after the claim can instead suppress unfinished work. For database effects, commit the unique claim and effect in the same transaction; external effects need provider-enforced idempotency and recovery of uncertain outcomes.

The ID must be stable across retries. Use a producer-assigned ID (an event ID or a business-operation key; orderId + eventType is only sufficient if that event type can occur once per order), **not** the broker's delivery ID, which may change on redelivery.

Keep deduplication state for the full permitted duplicate horizon, including delayed retries, archives and replay duration. Permanent business records may be appropriate when no reliable finite bound exists.



### 3. Version checks

For state updates, include a version or sequence number and apply only if it is newer:

The named values are application-bound parameters, not standalone PostgreSQL syntax. Inspect affected rows: a stale or equal version makes no change.

```sql
-- Replace only an older absolute snapshot.
UPDATE profiles SET email = :email,
       version = :v
 WHERE id = :id AND version < :v;
```

For absolute state snapshots with a single ordered version domain, this rejects stale updates. It does not safely skip missing deltas; initialise absent rows and coordinate versions across writers.

## Key takeaways

- Absolute state writes can be naturally idempotent, subject to stale updates and external side effects.
- Store a stable event or operation ID in the same database transaction as a non-idempotent effect.
- Deduplication retention must cover every permitted retry and replay, rather than only normal redelivery.
- Version checks protect snapshots from older writes; they do not safely skip missing deltas.

## Further reading

- [Idempotent Receiver (Enterprise Integration Patterns)](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/IdempotentReceiver.html)
- [Making retries safe with idempotent APIs (Amazon Builders' Library)](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/)
- [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)

questions.prompt: A consumer handles `PaymentReceived {paymentId, orderId, amount}` by running `UPDATE orders SET paid_total = paid_total + :amount`. Delivery is at-least-once. What is the risk, and what is the simplest robust change?

options.text: No risk; at-least-once delivery means each message is processed exactly once
options.explanation: Wrong. At-least-once explicitly permits duplicates. A redelivered message would add the amount a second time.

options.text: Duplicates will over-count; check a Redis set for the ID before updating and add it afterwards
options.explanation: Wrong. The check and the write are not atomic with the database update. A crash after the update but before the Redis write, or two concurrent deliveries, still double-counts.

options.text: Duplicates will over-count; record the payment ID in a processed table with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the update
options.explanation: Correct. The increment is not idempotent. Recording a stable payment ID atomically with the update makes a duplicate fail the unique insert and roll back, so the total changes once.

options.text: Messages may be lost; switch to at-most-once to be safe
options.explanation: Wrong. At-least-once does not lose messages; it duplicates them. At-most-once would make lost payments possible, which is worse.

questions.workedExample:
1. `paid_total + amount` applied twice adds twice: **not idempotent**.
2. Options, best first:
   - Make it absolute: store each payment as a row keyed by `paymentId` (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) and compute the total with `SUM`.
   - Or dedup: `INSERT INTO processed(payment_id)` plus the `UPDATE` in **one transaction**.
3. Walk through a duplicate: first delivery commits both. Second delivery's insert hits the primary key → rollback → consumer acks. Total unchanged.
4. The key requirement is **atomicity** between 'remember I did it' and 'do it'.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations are **naturally idempotent**, so a duplicate message causes no harm for the illustrated state effect, ignoring interleaved newer writes, triggers and external side effects? Select all that apply.

options.text: `UPDATE users SET email = 'a@x.com' WHERE id = 7`
options.explanation: Correct. Setting a field to an absolute value gives the same final state however many times it runs (ignoring interleaving with other updates).

options.text: `INSERT INTO orders(...) VALUES (...)` with an auto-increment primary key
options.explanation: Wrong. Each run creates a new row with a new ID, so duplicates create duplicate orders. Keying the insert on a natural or producer-supplied ID would fix this.

options.text: `PUT /carts/9/items/sku-1 {qty: 2}`
options.explanation: Correct. PUT replaces the resource with the given state; quantity is 2 after one call or ten.

options.text: Sending a push notification to a phone
options.explanation: Wrong. Each send produces another notification the user sees. A local sent record alone has a crash window around an external send; use provider-enforced deduplication or reconcile uncertain outcomes.

options.text: `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE id = 'abc'`
options.explanation: Correct. After the first delete the row is gone; later deletes affect zero rows and leave the same state.

questions.workedExample:
Test each by running it twice and comparing the end state with running it once:

| Op | Once | Twice | Same? |
|---|---|---|---|
| SET email | a@x | a@x | ✓ |
| INSERT auto-id | 1 row | 2 rows | ✗ |
| PUT qty 2 | 2 | 2 | ✓ |
| Push | 1 alert | 2 alerts | ✗ |
| DELETE | gone | gone | ✓ |

Design messages to carry **absolute state or stable keys** so consumers can use the idempotent forms.

questions.prompt: A producer publishes `RefundIssued` to an SQS standard queue and retries `SendMessage` whenever a call times out. The consumer deduplicates on the SQS `MessageId`, recording it in the same database transaction as the refund. Some refunds are still applied twice. Why?

options.text: SQS gives a redelivered message a new MessageId each time it is received
options.explanation: Wrong. A message keeps its MessageId across redeliveries; it is the **receipt handle** that changes on each receive. Broker redeliveries are caught by this dedup.

options.text: When a timed-out send had actually succeeded, the retry creates a second message with a different MessageId; dedup should use a producer-assigned ID such as the refund ID
options.explanation: Correct. SQS assigns MessageId when it accepts a message, so two successful sends of the same refund get two IDs and look unrelated. A stable, producer-assigned ID is the same for both copies.

options.text: SQS standard queues do not support deduplication, so consumer-side dedup cannot work
options.explanation: Wrong. Standard queues have no broker-side dedup, which is exactly why consumer-side dedup is needed. It works as long as it keys on an ID that is stable across producer retries.

options.text: The visibility timeout is too short
options.explanation: Wrong. A short visibility timeout causes broker redelivery of the same message, which keeps the same MessageId and would be caught by this dedup.

questions.workedExample:
Track the two kinds of duplicate:

| Source | MessageId |
|---|---|
| Broker redelivery | Same |
| Producer retry | **New** |

1. Producer sends; SQS stores it as `MessageId = A`; the response is lost.
2. Producer retries; SQS stores another copy, `MessageId = B`.
3. The consumer sees A and B as different and applies both.
4. Fix: the producer puts `refundId` (or an event UUID generated **once**, before the first attempt) in the message, and the consumer dedups on that.

questions.prompt: A Kafka consumer applies payments to Postgres with a dedup table whose rows expire after **1 hour**. The topic retains 7 days of data. During an incident, an operator resets the consumer group's offsets **3 days back** to reprocess possibly missed records. Afterwards, many payments have been applied twice. The team can enforce an audited finite bound on every allowed retry and replay path. How long should dedup records be kept?

options.text: 1 hour is fine; the operator should not have reset offsets
options.explanation: Wrong. Replaying from an earlier offset is a normal recovery tool for a log, and the consumer should survive it. The dedup window was too short for the duplicates the system can produce.

options.text: As long as `max.poll.interval.ms`, since that bounds how long a record can be in flight
options.explanation: Wrong. That covers only redelivery after a stuck consumer. Replays and late producer retries can bring back records from days earlier.

options.text: At least as long as a duplicate can plausibly arrive: here at least the documented replay/retry horizon, with a bound on deletion lag and replay duration
options.explanation: Correct. Any record still in the topic can be replayed, so dedup records must outlive it. A configured 7-day retention is not an exact deadline: segment deletion can lag and replays take time. An 8-day TTL is safe only if all permitted retry/replay paths are proven bounded by it.

options.text: Forever, because there is no safe bound
options.explanation: Wrong. Keeping them forever works but grows without limit. A finite bound requires an explicit replay/retry policy, including archives, republishing, segment deletion lag and replay duration; topic retention alone is insufficient.

questions.workedExample:
1. The replay returns records older than the dedup table remembers, so previously applied payments look new.
2. Retain dedup state for the full enforced duplicate horizon: retained records, delayed deletion, archives, producer retries and time spent replaying.
3. Topic retention alone is not a proven TTL for dedup records. If permitted replay is unbounded, permanent business records may be needed.
4. Expiring a large dedup table also needs care: PostgreSQL partitioned unique constraints must include the partition key, so time partitioning must not undermine payment-ID uniqueness.
5. A durable payment row keyed by payment ID can make the business effect naturally idempotent instead of relying on a short-lived side table.

lessons.title: Idempotency keys and producer retry limits
lessons.summary: Protect external effects and recognise the finite scope of broker-side deduplication.
lessons.body:
When a consumer calls another system, its local transaction cannot include that remote effect. The provider must recognise repeated attempts, and the caller must respect how long that recognition lasts.

## Idempotency keys for side effects

When the effect is a call to an external system (charging a card, sending an SMS), pass an **idempotency key** derived from the message. Stripe API v1, for example, accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header and returns the original result for a repeated key; it keeps keys for at least 24 hours. The external system does the dedup for you, but only within its own retention window, so a retry after pruning may be a fresh request. If the earlier outcome is uncertain, reconcile it before retrying outside that window.



## Producer-side duplicates

Duplicates also start at the producer. A publish times out, the producer retries, and the broker ends up with two copies.

- **SQS FIFO** deduplicates on `MessageDeduplicationId` (or a SHA-256 of the body with content-based deduplication) for a **5-minute** window.
- **Kafka idempotent producer** (default since 3.0): each producer has a producer ID and a per-partition sequence number. The broker rejects duplicates and out-of-order sequence numbers. This removes retry duplicates **within one producer session**, but a restarted producer gets a new ID.

## Key takeaways

- An external provider’s idempotency key must represent the same business operation on every attempt.
- A local claim row cannot alone make a remote effect atomic; retries still need the same provider key.
- Broker deduplication and provider keys have finite boundaries; uncertain outcomes beyond them need reconciliation.

## Further reading

- [Making retries safe with idempotent APIs (Amazon Builders' Library)](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/)
- [Stripe idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

questions.prompt: An SQS FIFO producer times out on `SendMessage` and retries **7 minutes later** with the same `MessageDeduplicationId`. The first attempt had actually succeeded. What happens?

options.text: SQS accepts the retry as a new message, so the consumer receives a duplicate
options.explanation: Correct. The deduplication window is 5 minutes. A retry outside it is treated as a fresh message, so the consumer must still be idempotent for late retries.

options.text: SQS discards the retry as a duplicate
options.explanation: Wrong. SQS FIFO deduplication only applies within a 5-minute interval. After 7 minutes the ID is no longer remembered.

options.text: SQS rejects the retry with an error
options.explanation: Wrong. Within the window SQS silently accepts the duplicate and does not deliver it; outside it, SQS accepts it as new. Neither case is an error.

options.text: SQS merges both messages into one
options.explanation: Wrong. Messages are never merged. Each is either deduplicated (dropped) or delivered.

questions.workedExample:
1. FIFO dedup: same `MessageDeduplicationId` within **5 minutes** → accepted but not delivered again.
2. Retry at 7 minutes: 7 > 5 → window expired → new message.
3. Consumer receives two messages with the same business content.
4. Lessons:
   - Broker dedup windows are finite; they cover quick retries, not slow ones.
   - Keep consumer-side dedup (keyed on the same ID) for as long as late duplicates are possible.
   - Retry promptly with backoff measured in seconds, not minutes, when relying on broker dedup.

questions.prompt: A consumer charges customers through Stripe API v1 when it receives `ChargeRequested {orderId, amount}` from an at-least-once queue. Assume one charge per order, identical request parameters, and all automatic retries occur within the provider's retained-key window. Which designs make duplicate delivery harmless? Select all that apply.

options.text: Acknowledge the message before calling Stripe, so it cannot be redelivered
options.explanation: Wrong. Acking first gives at-most-once: a crash after the ack but before the charge means the customer is never charged. Duplicates disappear only by accepting loss.

options.text: Send `Idempotency-Key: charge-<orderId>` with the request
options.explanation: Correct. The key is stable across redeliveries, so Stripe returns the original result for a repeated key instead of charging again. The external system does the dedup.

options.text: Check a Redis flag for the order, call Stripe, then set the flag
options.explanation: Wrong. Check-then-act is racy: two concurrent deliveries both see no flag, and a crash after the charge but before setting the flag also lets the next delivery charge again.

options.text: Insert a row into `charges(order_id UNIQUE)` before calling Stripe; if the row exists and is complete, skip; otherwise call Stripe with the same idempotency key
options.explanation: Correct. The unique insert is an atomic claim, and reusing the same idempotency key makes a retry after a crash safe. The row also gives you a local record of charge state.

options.text: Use the SQS receipt handle as the idempotency key
options.explanation: Wrong. The receipt handle changes on every receive, so each redelivery would present a new key and Stripe would charge again.

questions.workedExample:
1. The effect (a charge) lives in an **external** system, so a local transaction cannot cover it.
2. The tool is an **idempotency key** that is:
   - derived from business data (`orderId`), so it is identical on every delivery
   - sent on every attempt
3. A local claim row adds coordination and visibility, but must reuse the **same** key so a crash between claim and charge is safe on retry.
4. What fails:
   - early ack → possible loss
   - Redis check-then-set → race and crash window
   - receipt handle → changes per delivery

Remember the provider's window: Stripe API v1 keeps keys for at least 24 hours, so after the provider may have pruned the key, a completed local record can suppress retries, but an uncertain pending charge requires reconciliation with the provider before another charge is attempted.

lessons.title: Kafka transactions and exactly-once effect scope
lessons.summary: Make Kafka outputs and progress atomic while handling read isolation, fencing and external sinks.
lessons.body:
The familiar consume–process–produce loop has two outputs: its records and its progress. Kafka can commit those together, but work performed in another system needs a separate correctness argument.

## Kafka transactions: exactly-once within Kafka

Kafka's exactly-once semantics (EOS) target a specific pattern: **consume from Kafka, process, produce to Kafka** (read-process-write). The goal is that the output records and the consumer's offset commit happen atomically.

```
in-topic ─▶ app ─▶ out-topic
             │
             └─▶ offsets (same txn)
```

The following is a success-path sketch, not a complete runnable client. Configure a stable transactional.id, disable consumer auto-commit, return the next offset per partition from offsetsOf, and use read_committed for transactional inputs. Production code must abort/reseek on recoverable failure and close a fenced producer:

```java
// Fence older producers using this ID.
producer.initTransactions();
while (true) {
  var recs = consumer.poll(ofMillis(100));
  // Couple output records with progress.
  producer.beginTransaction();
  for (var r : recs)
    producer.send(transform(r));
  // offsetsOf returns the next read
  // offsets.
  producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(
      offsetsOf(recs),
      consumer.groupMetadata());
  // Commit records and offsets atomically.
  producer.commitTransaction();
}
```

How it works underneath:

1. A **transaction coordinator** (a broker) tracks the transaction in an internal `__transaction_state` log.
2. Output records are written to their partitions immediately but marked as part of an open transaction.
3. On commit, the coordinator writes **commit markers** to every partition involved, including `__consumer_offsets`.
4. Consumers with isolation.level=read_committed see non-transactional records and committed transactional records, up to the last stable offset. An earlier open transaction can delay later records. Aborted records are skipped. The Java consumer's default is `read_uncommitted`, so a downstream consumer that does not set this sees aborted output and loses the guarantee.

**Zombie fencing** handles the nasty case of a consumer that pauses (a long GC pause, say), is presumed dead and replaced, then wakes up and tries to write. Each `transactional.id` has a **producer epoch**; `initTransactions()` bumps it, and the broker rejects writes from the older epoch.

Kafka Streams wraps all of this behind one setting: `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`.

### What Kafka EOS does not cover

EOS is atomic only for **Kafka writes and Kafka offsets**. If your processing step also writes to Postgres, calls an API or sends an email, those effects are outside the transaction. An aborted and retried transaction will perform them again. For external sinks you are back to idempotent writes, or storing offsets in the same database transaction as the results:

This is schematic SQL: the ellipses omit the totals schema and aggregation. The ownership/expected-offset guard described below is also required; the sketch alone does not fence a stale consumer.

```sql
BEGIN;
-- Apply the batch to the external result.
INSERT INTO totals ... ON CONFLICT ...;
-- Store where this committed batch ends.
UPDATE kafka_offsets SET next = 1043
 WHERE topic='pay' AND part=3;
-- Result and position move together.
COMMIT;
```

On startup (and after every rebalance) the consumer reads `kafka_offsets` and calls `seek()` to that position instead of trusting `__consumer_offsets`. Results and position then move together. Also enforce ownership or the expected offset atomically in that transaction: after a rebalance, an old consumer can still be running, and storing offsets alone does not fence its writes.

Transaction commit coordination adds work, and read-committed visibility can add latency. Longer commit intervals can amortise coordination but delay visibility and increase recovery work. Measure the trade-off for the actual workload rather than assuming a universal overhead percentage.

## Choosing in practice

1. Default to **at-least-once** delivery.
2. Make every consumer **idempotent**: natural idempotence first, then dedup tables in the same transaction, then idempotency keys for external calls.
3. Use **Kafka transactions** (or Kafka Streams EOS) for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines where duplicates in output topics matter, such as financial aggregations.
4. Use **at-most-once** only where loss is acceptable and a duplicate is worse than nothing.

## Key takeaways

- Kafka transactions combine output records and consumed offsets; readers need read_committed to hide aborted output.
- A newer producer epoch fences a paused older producer using the same transactional identity.
- External database/API effects need their own idempotence or atomic results-plus-offsets design with an ownership guard.
- Exactly-once is a boundary to design and test, rather than a promise that covers every side effect.

## Further reading

- [Exactly-once semantics are possible: here's how Kafka does it (Confluent)](https://www.confluent.io/blog/exactly-once-semantics-are-possible-heres-how-apache-kafka-does-it/)
- [Transactions in Apache Kafka (Confluent)](https://www.confluent.io/blog/transactions-apache-kafka/)
- [Kafka message delivery semantics (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/kafka/design/delivery-semantics.html)
- [Kafka 4.2 producer API](https://kafka.apache.org/42/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/producer/KafkaProducer.html)

questions.prompt: A Kafka Streams app reads `payments`, aggregates per merchant, and writes to `merchant-totals` with `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2`. It also calls an external fraud API for each payment. After a broker restart, the fraud team reports some payments were **scored twice**. The totals are correct. Explain.

options.text: exactly_once_v2 is buggy; switch back to at_least_once
options.explanation: Wrong. at_least_once would make things worse: the totals could also double-count. The behaviour is the expected limit of EOS, not a bug.

options.text: Kafka EOS makes Kafka writes and offset commits atomic, but external calls are outside the transaction, so an aborted and retried transaction repeats them
options.explanation: Correct. When a transaction aborts, its output records are discarded for read_committed consumers and the input is reprocessed. Kafka cannot undo an HTTP call, so the fraud API sees it twice. Pass an idempotency key (such as the payment ID) to the API.

options.text: The fraud API received duplicates because read_committed was not set on the producer
options.explanation: Wrong. isolation.level is a consumer setting, and it governs which Kafka records are visible. It has no effect on HTTP calls made during processing.

options.text: The broker restart caused unclean leader election, which duplicated input records
options.explanation: Wrong. Unclean election can lose data, not duplicate it, and it is disabled by default. Correct totals alone do not prove absence of input duplication; the stated failure is consistent with transaction retries outside the external API boundary.

questions.workedExample:
1. Transaction T reads offsets 500–599, calls fraud API for each, writes totals, then tries to commit.
2. Suppose the failure causes T to abort (a restart alone does not imply every transaction aborts).
3. Kafka's view: aborted output is invisible to `read_committed` readers; offsets were not committed → reprocess 500–599. **Totals stay correct.**
4. Fraud API's view: it already received 100 calls from the aborted attempt, and now receives them again. **Duplicates.**
5. Fix: send `Idempotency-Key: payment-<id>` so the API returns the earlier score, or move the call into a separate consumer that uses provider-enforced idempotency and reconciles uncertain outcomes. A local dedup record alone cannot atomically cover an external API call.

questions.prompt: In a transactional Kafka read-process-write app, instance A pauses for 60 seconds in a GC pause. The group rebalances and instance B takes over A's partitions with the same transactional.id and successfully calls initTransactions(). A then wakes up and tries to commit its open transaction. What happens?

options.text: Both A's and B's outputs are committed, producing duplicates
options.explanation: Wrong. This is exactly the zombie scenario that transactional IDs are designed to prevent.

options.text: A's commit succeeds and B's transaction is aborted instead
options.explanation: Wrong. Fencing always favours the newer epoch. Letting the older instance win would allow a paused zombie to overwrite the current owner's work.

options.text: A's commit is rejected because B's initTransactions() bumped the producer epoch, fencing A
options.explanation: Correct. The coordinator tracks an epoch per transactional.id. B's initTransactions() incremented it and aborted A's open transaction; A's requests carry the old epoch and fail with a fencing error.

options.text: The consumer group blocks until A either commits or times out
options.explanation: Wrong. The rebalance already completed when A missed its deadline. B proceeds; Kafka does not wait for A.

questions.workedExample:
1. A: `transactional.id = app-p3`, epoch 5. Opens transaction, writes some output.
2. A pauses; the group gives P3 to B.
3. B calls `initTransactions()` with `app-p3` → coordinator **aborts** any open transaction for that ID and bumps the epoch to 6.
4. A wakes and sends commit with epoch 5 → `ProducerFencedException`. A must shut down.
5. Result: A's partial output is aborted (invisible to read_committed), and B reprocesses from the last committed offset, so each input produces output once.

(Since KIP-447, fencing also uses the consumer group generation, so apps no longer need a static transactional.id per partition.)

questions.prompt: A consumer reads `payments` from Kafka and adds each amount to a `merchant_totals` row in Postgres. It commits offsets to Kafka **after** the database transaction commits. After crashes, totals are occasionally too high. Without using Kafka transactions, which design gives exactly-once effects?

options.text: Store the partition's next offset in Postgres in the same transaction as the totals update, atomically guard that update by the expected previous offset or ownership epoch, and on startup/rebalance seek to the stored offset
options.explanation: Correct. Totals and position now commit atomically in one database, so after a crash the consumer resumes exactly where its last applied batch ended. Kafka's own committed offsets are no longer the source of truth.

options.text: Turn on `exactly_once_v2` or Kafka transactions for the consumer
options.explanation: Wrong. Kafka transactions make Kafka writes and Kafka offset commits atomic. The Postgres update is outside them, so a crash between the database commit and the offset commit still replays the batch.

options.text: Commit offsets to Kafka before the database transaction
options.explanation: Wrong. That swaps duplicates for loss: a crash after the offset commit but before the database commit skips the batch.

options.text: Set `isolation.level=read_committed` on the consumer
options.explanation: Wrong. That only hides records from aborted Kafka transactions on the input. It does nothing about the gap between the Postgres commit and the offset commit.

questions.workedExample:
1. Find the gap: `COMMIT` in Postgres → crash → offset never committed → batch replayed → totals added twice.
2. Close it by putting both in **one** database, updated in one transaction:

This is application-bound SQL: substitute parameters and enforce the affected-row rollback check in the driver.

```sql
BEGIN;
-- Apply the batch's external effect.
UPDATE merchant_totals
  SET total = total + :amt
  WHERE id = :m;
-- Claim progress only from our start.
UPDATE kafka_offsets SET next = :o
  WHERE topic = 'payments'
    AND part = :p AND next = :expected;
-- If row count != 1: ROLLBACK.
-- Commit the guarded result and offset.
COMMIT;
```

3. On partition assignment, read `kafka_offsets` and `seek(partition, next)`.
4. Atomically require the expected offset/ownership guard to match; roll back both changes otherwise. With this guard, a stale consumer cannot apply the batch twice. Crash anywhere: either both updates committed (resume after the batch) or neither did (replay it). Each payment counts once.
5. This is the "store offsets with the results" pattern the lesson mentions for external sinks.

questions.prompt: A Kafka Streams app with `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2` writes invoices to an `invoices` topic. Another team's plain Java consumer of `invoices`, built with default settings, sometimes receives duplicate invoices after broker restarts. Reading the same topic with a `read_committed` consumer shows no duplicates. What is the cause?

options.text: The Streams app's idempotent producer is disabled
options.explanation: Wrong. exactly_once_v2 requires and enables idempotence and transactions. The fact that a read_committed reader sees clean output shows the producer side is working.

options.text: Unclean leader election duplicated records during the restart
options.explanation: Wrong. Unclean election can lose records; it does not duplicate them, and it is off by default. A read_committed reader would also see any such problem.

options.text: The other team's consumer group has more members than partitions
options.explanation: Wrong. Extra members sit idle; they never share a partition or cause duplicates.

options.text: The Java consumer defaults to `isolation.level=read_uncommitted`, so it also reads output from transactions that were later aborted and retried
options.explanation: Correct. When a transaction aborts, its records stay in the log with an abort marker, and the retry writes them again. Only read_committed consumers skip the aborted copy. Exactly-once output needs read_committed readers.

questions.workedExample:
1. Transaction T1 writes invoices 1–50, then suppose a broker failure causes T1 to abort.
2. The records from T1 remain in the log, followed by an **abort marker**.
3. The Streams app retries in T2 and writes invoices 1–50 again, then commits.
4. A `read_committed` consumer skips T1's records → each invoice once.
5. A `read_uncommitted` consumer (the Java client default) returns T1's and T2's records → duplicates.
6. Fix: set `isolation.level=read_committed` on every consumer of transactional topics. Expect slightly higher latency, since records become visible only at commit.

lessons.title: Per-entity ordering and hot-key capacity
lessons.summary: Choose the smallest ordered entity, then diagnose skew and shard limits.
lessons.body:
Two problems dominate real messaging systems once they are past the prototype stage. First, **ordering**: some messages must be applied in sequence, yet you want hundreds of consumers in parallel. Second, **flow control**: producers and consumers run at different speeds, and something has to give. This unit starts with ordering and hot keys. Later units cover flow control and the operational signal that ties them together: **consumer lag**.

## How much ordering do you need?

Global ordering (every message in one sequence) requires a common sequencing/coordination point, though ordered execution and replication can still use multiple machines. That rarely scales. Almost every real requirement is **per-entity ordering**: events for one account, one order, or one device must be in order, but events for different entities are independent.

```
acct A: open ─▶ deposit ─▶ close
acct B: open ─▶ withdraw
  (A and B may interleave freely)
```

The tool for this is a **partition key** (Kafka, Kinesis) or a **message group ID** (SQS FIFO, Azure Service Bus sessions). All messages with the same key go to the same ordered lane, and different keys spread across lanes.

| System | Ordered unit | Parallelism |
|---|---|---|
| Kafka | Partition | Partitions per group |
| Kinesis | Shard | Shards |
| SQS FIFO | Message group | Number of groups |
| Service Bus | Session | Number of sessions |

For sustained provisioned-shard sizing without record aggregation, a Kinesis shard supports 1 MB/s **or** 1,000 records per second of writes, whichever comes first, and shared GetRecords reads have a 2 MB/s shard limit (enhanced fan-out has per-consumer capacity), so you size shards on both bytes and record count and take the larger answer:

```formula reference
S = ⌈max(W / (1 MB/s), R / (1000/s))⌉
where
S: the minimum number of shards
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to the next whole number, because you cannot have part of a shard
max: the larger of the values inside the brackets
W: the bytes written per second, here 4,000 records of 500 bytes, which is 2 MB/s
R: the records written per second, here 4,000
MB: megabytes; "MB/s" means megabytes per second
s: seconds; "/s" means per second
In words: work out how many shards the byte rate needs and how many the record rate needs, and provision the larger number.
```

Small records hit the record limit first and large records hit the byte limit first. Both limits apply to each shard, so a hot partition key can overload one shard even when the stream's average is fine.

This estimate assumes evenly distributed keys, no record aggregation and sustained rates. Add headroom and check actual shard metrics; a stream-wide average can hide an overloaded shard.

SQS FIFO is notable: it does not lock a whole partition. A single receive can return multiple messages in group order-17; additional receives for that group wait until the in-flight messages are deleted or visible again, but any other group can be served. So parallelism scales with the number of **active groups**, not a fixed partition count.

## Hot keys and skew

Hashing spreads keys evenly only if traffic per key is even. It rarely is. If one celebrity account produces 30% of events, the partition holding that key gets 30% of the load, and its consumer becomes the bottleneck no matter how many others you add.

Mitigations:

- **Pick a finer key.** Order by `conversationId` rather than `userId` if that is what ordering really needs.
- **Salt the hot key.** Spread `celebrity-1` across `celebrity-1#0`…`#7`, accepting that ordering is now only within each sub-key, and merge downstream.
- **Separate topic.** Route known heavy hitters to a dedicated, bigger pipeline.

## Key takeaways

- Per-entity lanes allow unrelated entities to run in parallel.
- Provisioned Kinesis shards must satisfy both byte-rate and record-rate limits.
- A hot key stays on one lane; finer keys, salting or dedicated pipelines can remove that bottleneck.
- Salt only when the required order permits it, and combine partial aggregates without counting an update twice.

## Further reading

- [Kinesis quotas and limits (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/service-sizes-and-limits.html)
- [Amazon SQS FIFO queues (AWS docs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues.html)
- [Kafka consumer (Confluent docs)](https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/clients/consumer.html)

questions.prompt: An SQS FIFO queue carries order events with `MessageGroupId = orderId`. There are 10,000 groups with available work and 50 single-job consumers. Ignore quotas and receive-distribution limitations. How much parallelism can the consumers achieve?

options.text: Up to 50, because there are many more active groups than consumers
options.explanation: Correct. SQS holds back further messages only for a group with a message in flight. With 10,000 groups, there is enough independent group work for up to 50 consumers to work on (subject to FIFO throughput limits).

options.text: 1, because FIFO queues process one message at a time
options.explanation: Wrong. FIFO ordering applies within each message group, not across the whole queue. Different groups can be processed concurrently.

options.text: Up to 10,000, one per order
options.explanation: Wrong. 10,000 groups could support 10,000 concurrent consumers, but you have only 50. Parallelism is the minimum of available consumers and active groups.

options.text: It depends on the number of partitions configured on the queue
options.explanation: Wrong. SQS FIFO queues have no user-configured partitions like Kafka. Parallelism is driven by message groups.

questions.workedExample:
1. Within a message group, preserve effect order. One receive can include several same-group records, and further receives wait for deletion or visibility expiry.
2. Different groups can proceed independently.
3. There are more ready groups than workers in this scenario, so every worker can have independent work. The worker fleet is the stated limit.
4. A single constant group ID would remove that independence. Real deployments must also check FIFO throughput limits and receive behaviour.

questions.prompt: A chat app uses `userId` as the Kafka key for message events. One celebrity user generates 35% of all traffic across thousands of similarly active conversations. Their partition's consumer is pinned at 100% CPU and lagging, while others idle. Ordering is only needed **within a conversation**. What is the best change?

options.text: Change the key to conversationId
options.explanation: Correct. Ordering is required per conversation, not per user. The celebrity takes part in thousands of conversations, so keying by conversation spreads their load across all partitions while keeping each conversation in order.

options.text: Add more partitions so the celebrity's traffic is spread out
options.explanation: Wrong. All records with one key hash to one partition however many partitions exist. More partitions spread other users but leave the celebrity's 35% on a single partition.

options.text: Remove the key so records are spread round-robin
options.explanation: Wrong. That fixes the skew but loses ordering within conversations, which is a stated requirement.

options.text: Give that one consumer a bigger machine
options.explanation: Wrong. Vertical scaling buys a little time, but 35% of all traffic will keep growing on one partition and one thread. The key choice is the root cause.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Find the real ordering requirement**: messages in one conversation must be in order. Messages across conversations need not be.
2. **Current key** (`userId`) is coarser than needed, so one heavy user maps to one partition.
3. **Finer key** (`conversationId`): the celebrity's 35% is split across, say, 5,000 conversations, which hash across all 48 partitions → roughly 0.7% each from that user.
4. **Check the new risk**: a single huge group conversation could become a hot key itself. Route a still-hot conversation to a dedicated pipeline or increase its lane capacity. Salting would weaken the stated conversation-order requirement and needs an explicit reordering protocol.
5. Remember that changing the key mid-stream can reorder in-flight conversations; use an explicit migration barrier/drain or sequence-aware merge. A quiet time alone is not a correctness guarantee.

questions.prompt: A pipeline counts likes per post, keyed by `postId`, on a 48-partition topic. A viral post sends 40% of all events to one partition, whose consumer is saturated. The count is a sum, so the order of likes does not matter. What is the best change?

options.text: Salt the hot key: send its events to `postId#0` … `postId#15` at random, count each sub-key, and sum the partial counts downstream
options.explanation: Correct. Because the aggregate is a sum, ordering across sub-keys does not matter. Sixteen sub-keys spread the viral post over up to 16 partitions, and a small second stage adds the partials.

options.text: Add more partitions
options.explanation: Wrong. Every event with the same key hashes to the same partition, however many partitions exist. More partitions spread other posts but leave the viral one where it is.

options.text: Move the viral post to an SQS FIFO queue with `MessageGroupId = postId`
options.explanation: Wrong. One message group is processed strictly in sequence, so this reproduces the same single-lane bottleneck in a different system.

options.text: Give the hot partition's consumer a bigger machine
options.explanation: Wrong. It buys a little time, but one consumer thread is still handling 40% of all traffic, and the next viral post may be bigger.

questions.workedExample:
1. **What ordering is needed?** None: addition is commutative.
2. So the single-key constraint is self-imposed. Salt it:

This Python fragment requires `import random` and an existing `post_id`. The chosen suffix is random, so it has no fixed output.

```python
# Choose one of 16 sub-keys for this
# like.
salt = random.randrange(16)
# Route using the finer, salted key.
key = f"{post_id}#{salt}"
```

3. Stage 1 counts per salted key (spread over up to 16 partitions).
4. Stage 2 re-keys by `postId` and combines 16 partial counts without double-counting updates: replace each versioned partial snapshot or apply deduplicated deltas. That stage handles one small update per sub-key per window, not every like.
5. Salts can collide on the same partition, and unrelated traffic adds load. Check actual partition distribution rather than assuming every salt gets a separate lane.
6. Salt only keys known or detected to be hot, so normal posts are unaffected.

questions.prompt: A provisioned Kinesis stream uses balanced partition keys and no record aggregation. Write requests for many tiny records are throttled even though each shard's byte rate is below its limit. Monitoring shows shards have reached their permitted records-per-second rate. What explains this?

options.text: Byte capacity is the only write limit, so this must be a monitoring error
options.explanation: Wrong. Both byte throughput and record count constrain sustained writes.

options.text: Small records cannot be throttled
options.explanation: Wrong. Small records can reach the count limit before exhausting byte capacity.

options.text: The shared read limit must be blocking the producer
options.explanation: Wrong. The stated evidence identifies the write record-count limit; read throughput is a separate constraint.

options.text: The record-count limit is binding before the byte limit
options.explanation: Correct. Capacity planning must satisfy both limits per shard. For the stated balanced unaggregated workload, more shard capacity can help; do not size from bytes alone.

questions.workedExample:
1. Check both write dimensions: bytes per second and records per second.
2. Tiny records use little byte capacity per request, so many can exhaust the record allowance while byte capacity remains.
3. Plan against whichever limit demands more shards, add headroom and inspect per-shard distribution.
4. More total capacity cannot cure a single hot key automatically. Aggregation changes the record-count calculation and needs its own design.
